approach_variants.name: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is the same day out as the Southwest Ridge route on this peak and the two describe substantially the same ground. From the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,600 ft, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col. Tepeh Towers are passed along this same traverse. From the col, follow the ridge line along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where the standard sequence is a rappel of about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier, then a traverse high and left across it toward Austera. This is meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado, and it is worth saying plainly: this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak, despite the catalog filing several of these objectives out of the same area. Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête, not a free-standing summit, and it is the most accessible top in that group — which is exactly why parties end up on the wrong one.
approach_variants.season: Aug is the usual window; the timing is set by the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers being safely negotiable rather than by the rock
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glacier traverses
A moat at the rappel point that has to work in both directions
Loose rock on the final summit tower
Rime or verglas on the final chimney even in summer
Exposed climbing on the closing pitches above a remote glacier, with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft that you rappel into, not walk through. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

Get there by counting, not by sighting Austera. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your left through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the second break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

Above the glacier traverse the climbing is short and countable: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a sub-summit, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, swinging right onto the northeast face — reaches the true top.

The false summit is the real hazard on this peak, and it is the test that matters. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. The true summit is reached only after crossing a narrow, often snowy ridge between two blocks and climbing a short chimney or a few feet of low fifth beyond it. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The moat beside the rappel point is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel with potholes and washboard; passenger cars can often reach mile ~18 (NP boundary) but a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for the final miles to the Eldorado TH/Boston Basin pulloff (~mile 20-21.7). waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH
waypoints.note: Large pullout at mile 20 of Cascade River Road; cross the Cascade River on a log/flagged crossing to the climbers' trail.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road south about 20 miles to the parking area near mile 20 — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard after that. Any overnight needs a free North Cascades backcountry permit, reserved in advance on Recreation.gov or drawn from the walk-up allocation in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the Inspiration Glacier flat used as base for Eldorado's satellite peaks.
waypoints.directions: Backtrack a short distance along the road from the lot to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River — historically a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts from year to year. On the far side a steep, unmaintained climbers' path gains 3,000-3,500 ft through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek and opens into the meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, then continues onto glacier to the camp on the Inspiration flat. Figure 5-6 hours from the car, with roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear needed above the meadows.

waypoints.name: Klawatti col
waypoints.note: Break in the ridge above the McAllister Glacier; rappel ~75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier northeast at roughly 7,800 ft, continuing well past Eldorado's own summit and the Tepeh Towers to the col on Klawatti's flank. Go through the col and follow Klawatti's north ridge across the upper McAllister Glacier area up to the gap in the ridge at about 7,900 ft.

waypoints.name: Klawatti Glacier crevasses
waypoints.note: Traverse high and left across the crevassed Klawatti Glacier toward Austera.
waypoints.directions: Work through the moat below the break — usually straightforward by August, more of a problem early season or in a heavy snow year — then rappel about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier. Leave a retrievable cordelette rather than fixed gear, since the exit reverses this pitch on lead at about 5.5. Rope up again and traverse the glacier high and climber's left toward Austera; the Klawatti has receded a great deal, so expect the crossing to be more broken than older descriptions suggest, and the peak itself does not resolve until you are close.

waypoints.name: Austera Peak
waypoints.note: Final 30 ft of low 5th-class climbing on the northeast face.
waypoints.directions: Leave the glacier where the traverse runs out below the peak and scramble 4th class for a few hundred feet, then angle left and traverse a broken ridge to the sub-summit. A final short pitch of well-protected low 5th class swings right onto the northeast face to the true summit; the rock on the summit tower is loose enough to be worth belaying.

approach_variants.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
approach_variants.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
approach_variants.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
hazards: Icefall traversed on the approach; crevasse and serac fall, and the crossing is described as frightening
Crumbly red rock band across the whole face at mid-height is the source of rockfall
Extreme remoteness; an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed is very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground compound the difficulty
Narrow season window depending on a bridged icefall and residual snow in the summit gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: The sequence is countable from bottom to top and it is the best thing this route has: easier cliffs, then a small glacier, then left up it to an icefall, then right through the icefall to the rock. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one. The rope-up point is a ledge system near the second prominent tree, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible. The mid-route confirmation is a colour and it crosses the whole face: a prominent, crumbly red stratum at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting. Between those two, follow the prominent central rib essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-ft notch is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit. And the negative test is the whole peak: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.notes: Reach the Stehekin valley by boat and the valley shuttle, or on foot over Cascade Pass, then walk or bike the washed-out upper valley road to the Park Creek trailhead. The Park Creek trail climbs toward Park Creek Pass, and the face sits at the head of the valley below the pass. Much less walking than Thunder Creek once you are in the valley.
hazards: Icefall traversed above the small glacier; crevasse and serac fall
Crumbly red rock band across the face at mid-height is the source of rockfall
Extreme remoteness; an incident on this face is very hard to get help for
Boat and shuttle schedules; a missed connection can cost a day
Washed-out upper valley road before the Park Creek trailhead
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When you reach the area through Stehekin, by boat or over Cascade Pass, since it means far less walking than the Thunder Creek approach once you are in the valley.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass, the sandy gully and the rocky point, then up to the Booker-Buckner col
approach_variants.notes:
The usual approach is a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass — on the order of forty miles round trip with roughly 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — or as a leg of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass, Buckner and Park Creek Pass.

From a camp near Park Creek Pass, this is a short day. Hike about 0.4 mile north on the Thunder Creek trail, pick up the climber's track, and traverse northeast: cross a broad sandy gully at about 6,900 ft, roughly a mile from the pass, continue toward a sharp rocky point at about 7,760 ft, then turn right and uphill on talus and snow to the col and its small glacier.

The col is around 8,100 ft and the scramble above it is class 2-3 with no technical rock. Booker sees roughly one party a year, so expect no boot track and no cairns.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, when the snowbridges near the Booker-Buckner col are still intact but consolidated. Conditions change year to year and can degrade within days
hazards: Crevasses and a bergschrund at the Booker-Buckner col, bypassed only on snowbridges of variable reliability — one such bridge collapsed within a week of another party crossing it, with climbers on both sides
Loose blocks in the summit gully, with rockfall released by climbers above as the route's principal hazard
Slick meltwater-run rock slabs for parties coming in from the Horseshoe Basin side
A remote, multi-day position far from any road or quick rescue
No boot track and no cairns — the route is walked by about one party a year
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route is navigated by a chain of three positions rather than one landmark, and the chain is countable in fog: a broad sandy gully at about 6,900 ft, roughly a mile from Park Creek Pass. Then a sharp, rocky point at about 7,760 ft. Then turn right and uphill to the col. Miss the gully and you are too low; pass the rocky point without turning and you are traversing past the peak.

The base is the Booker-Buckner Col at about 8,100 ft, and it is the col rather than the summit that the whole day is about: the upper snow and the glacier margin below it hold the crevasses, and the same snowbridges have to work on the way back down. Sound them, cross early while frozen, and note where you crossed.

Above the col, a north-facing gully leads toward the summit with one short class 3 step. Keep to one side of it rather than the gut, and do not stack the party one above another.

The route-finding trap is at the top and it is specific: leaving the gully too early puts you above a short wall on the west, and forces an awkward traverse back on small ledges. Cut right out of the gully onto low-angle talus and scree, and walk those to the summit. If you find yourself edging along small ledges above a wall, you exited one notch too soon.

Tell it from the peak's other walk-up by height: the South Ridge is gained across Horseshoe Basin at a permanent snowfield around 7,000-7,200 ft and trends to the ridge west of the summit. This route goes a thousand feet higher, to the col between Booker and Buckner. If you never got above 7,500 ft before starting to climb, you are on the South Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Horseshoe Basin at 6,400-6,600 ft to the north-facing gully and the permanent snowfield
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike the Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then continue up the Sahale Arm trail toward Sahale Glacier and Sahale Camp.

Leave the maintained trail near Sahale Camp and descend cross-country into Horseshoe Basin by a snow-free gully on Sahale's south side around 6,600 ft. Traverse the basin staying roughly between 6,400 and 6,600 ft, past the Buckner buttress.

Most parties combine Booker with Buckner on the same trip, since both share this approach and this traverse. Route-finding through Horseshoe Basin is the crux of the day; the climbing is not.
approach_variants.season: July through September, after Cascade River Road opens and once Horseshoe Basin's snowfields have consolidated; early attempts face more snow travel and less obvious route-finding, late ones find slopes melted to loose scree and slab
hazards: Loose scree and slabby terrain throughout Horseshoe Basin, easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands flanking the south ridge that have to be route-found around
Rockfall potential in the gullies flanking the ridge
A remote position with no cell coverage and very infrequent traffic if a rescue is needed
A cross-country traverse and an exposed summit gully that are far more hazardous to reverse in the dark or after a thunderstorm has softened the snowfields
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a north-facing rock gully and a permanent snowfield at about 7,000-7,200 ft, reached by crossing Horseshoe Basin rather than by climbing to any col. The snowfield is the marker: it is permanent, so it is there whatever the month, and the gully leads off it to the south-trending ridge west of Booker's summit.

The height is the test that separates this route from its neighbour, and it is a thousand feet wide. The Northwest Route starts at the Booker-Buckner Col at about 8,100 ft, reached from Park Creek Pass by way of a sandy gully at 6,900 ft and a sharp rocky point at 7,760 ft. This route starts a thousand feet lower and on the other side. If you are standing at a col between two peaks, you are not on the South Ridge.

The approach test is that you go down before you go up: from Sahale Camp you descend Sahale's south side through a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin and traverse at 6,400-6,600 ft. If your day has been a continuous climb from the trailhead, you have not reached the basin traverse yet.

The finish is short and exposed and it is the one piece of real climbing: talus and slabs give way to a short, somewhat exposed 3rd-class gully or dike — locally described as taking a 4th-class step — to the summit.

What is honestly thin here: this ridge is barely documented. The only outside mention found is of a party who abandoned the South Ridge for loose terrain and moved to the Northwest Route, finding existing rappel slings on the ridge — which suggests it is sometimes retreated from rather than climbed. Treat the snowfield and the gully as the navigation and expect to do your own route-finding above them.

waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass Trailhead at about 3,600 ft; it is paved to start and gravel the rest of the way. The season here runs July through September and depends on Cascade River Road being open, so check that before you make the drive. Most parties climb this as one very long day from the lot, leaving the car around 2-3 am; if you would rather split it, the overnights at Pelton Basin and Sahale Glacier Camp are permitted camps, so sort the permit out before you drive.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.directions: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up long switchbacks through forest and then across open slopes, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain, to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft.

waypoints.name: Booker Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: Continue up the Sahale Arm trail toward Sahale Glacier Camp. Near the camp leave the trail and descend Sahale's south side by a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin, then traverse the basin at 6,400-6,600 ft past the Buckner buttress to a permanent snowfield and north-facing gully at 7,000-7,200 ft. Above, talus and slabs on the south ridge lead to a short, exposed 3rd-class gully and the summit.

approach_variants.name: The Quien Sabe's northwest corner to the lower of the two gullies
approach_variants.notes:
In winter the recorded approach is Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead gate, then bike or ski up the Cascade Pass trail to the highest switchback, angling up to about 6,400 ft and dropping into the Soldier Boy drainage, then a rising traverse to the Quien Sabe Glacier's northwest corner. Rope up for the glacier crossing. In summer the standard Boston Basin approach reaches the same ground.

The face is used deliberately as the lower-consequence alternative to the Southeast Face when that side is too icy and too unprotected — which is worth knowing, because it means a party may arrive here having changed its mind rather than having planned it.

Five pitches: two of steep snow heading northeast, a large gully east on the third, a fourth to about 200 ft north of the summit, and a fifth across an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top.
approach_variants.season: Condition-dependent rather than calendar-dependent — documented ascents span a September first ascent on steep snow and a February first winter ascent
hazards: A bergschrund near the base of the face
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe Glacier approach
Rime ice needing removal before anything can be climbed or protected, on the winter ascent
Rock bands between the gullies that are poor rock and poor protection — the gullies themselves protect better than the face between them
Loose rock characteristic of this peak, especially on the summit rock step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Count the gullies: there are two prominent ones on this face and the route takes the lower. That is the one countable fact published about the start and it is the one to carry. A party at the base of the other gully is on a different piece of the face, with the rock band between them as the divider.

The first-move test is the schrund, and its solution is directional: the bergschrund at the base is turned by climbing to climber's right. If your way past the schrund went left, re-examine which gully you are under.

Count the first two belays, which are described by what they sit under rather than by height: two pitches of steep snow head northeast, the first belay under a bulge and the second where a gully opens to the east. If your second stance is not at a place where a gully opens away east, the line is wrong.

And you are on the wrong side of the mountain if you crossed a col. The Southeast Face — the standard route — is reached over the Sahale-Boston col at about 8,200 ft and shares that saddle with the Sahale trade route. This face is climbed straight off the northwest corner of the Quien Sabe with no col crossed at all. If you walked over a saddle to get where you are standing, you are under the standard route, not this one.

The finish confirms it: pitch four tops out about 200 ft north of the summit and the last pitch crosses an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top. A route that deposits you on the summit directly has not been this one.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Open to the Cascade Pass trailhead as of July 2026; spring-2026 landslide damage near MP 18 kept it gated at the Eldorado Trailhead (MP 20) into June
road.driveNote: In winter/spring conditions, expect to approach entirely from the Eldorado gate on skis or foot — no vehicle access beyond MP 20.
road.seasonalGate: Typically gated in winter/spring; the documented winter ascent approached from this same Eldorado gate on skis/bike

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 at Marblemount, take Cascade River Road east across the Skagit River and follow it about 20 miles to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at milepost 20. From late autumn to spring the road is gated here, three miles below its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead; foot and bicycle traffic may continue past the gate.

waypoints.name: Winter approach angle point (~6,400 ft)
waypoints.directions: Bike, walk or ski the road beyond the gate to the Cascade Pass trailhead, climb the Cascade Pass Trail to its highest switchback, then leave the trail and angle up the slope to the northeast to about 6,400 ft.

waypoints.name: West Face route start
waypoints.directions: Drop into the Soldier Boy drainage and make a rising traverse to the northwest corner of the Quien Sabe Glacier. Rope up and cross the glacier to the foot of the west face, below the lower of its two prominent gullies; the bergschrund at the base is turned on climber's right.

waypoints.name: Boston Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb two pitches of steep snow heading northeast, belaying first under a bulge and then where a gully opens to the east. Follow that large gully east on the third pitch, climb a fourth pitch to about 200 ft north of the summit, then cross the exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Winter approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Trailhead gate

access.fees: No fee for day use; overnight backcountry permits cost roughly $10/person per night plus a one-time $6 nonrefundable reservation fee, charged only in the summer season (mid-May-early October) — free the rest of the year.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the eleven named cross-country zones — Boston Basin, Eldorado, Forbidden, Hidden Lake, Icy, Inspiration, Nooksack, Price, Sulphide Glacier, Torment Basin and Triad — one of which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Wilderness permit required for overnight stays. Sahale Glacier Camp and Cascade Pass camps are among the most in-demand sites in the park; 60% of permits are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (Early-Access lottery in Feb-Mar, general on-sale in spring), and 40% are held for walk-up. Permits must be picked up/activated in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day of or day before the trip.
access.closures: Cascade River Road (FR-15) is typically snow-gated in winter and spring and may not open to the trailhead until early-mid summer; it has also suffered repeated storm washouts in recent years (e.g., August 2025). Check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

Permits reached from Cascade River Road must be picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.
approach_variants.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the bergschrund at the toe of the face, on the Boston Glacier, and the position test is directional: from the col you traverse south across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

The entry move is a zig-zag and it is the positive test: work climber's left of the bergschrund, then back right into the centre of the lower face, and then straight up. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

What you are climbing confirms it: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

The finish is the other countable point, and getting it wrong costs time at the worst moment: continue straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse to the left. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

And the approach itself is the strongest negative test against this peak's other route: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. If you walked past an old mine in a basin at 7,000 ft, you are on the southwest route.

approach_variants.name: Over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp
approach_variants.notes: A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
approach_variants.whyThisWay: To skip the rappel onto the Boston Glacier from Sharkfin Col; the Sahale side is reached from Cascade Pass and camps at Sahale Glacier Camp or the col, but it is a longer way round.

road.name: Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15)
road.status: Gravel, summer-passable
road.driveNote: Rough, washboarded gravel for the final miles to the Cascade Pass Trailhead, about 22.9-23 miles from Marblemount; has experienced washouts requiring temporary closures in recent years.
road.seasonalGate: Snow closure in winter/spring; opening date varies year to year with snowpack and road damage.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road (FR-15) at about 3,200 ft. The unmaintained climbers' path follows an old mining road about a mile, then climbs steeply through old growth into Boston Basin; wilderness permit required for overnight camping, and Boston Basin camping is limited to its two designated camps.
waypoints.directions: Cascade River Road (FR-15) runs east from Marblemount; the trailhead is a small pullout at about mile 21.7, a couple of miles short of the Cascade Pass road-end loop where the Sahale Arm exit comes out. The upper road is narrow gravel and holds snow into early summer.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: On the Sahale Arm way in or out: leave the Cascade Pass trail here and climb the Sahale Arm climbers' path north toward Sahale Glacier Camp.
waypoints.directions: From the Cascade Pass road-end loop, a couple of miles past the Boston Basin pullout, the maintained trail switchbacks up through forest, roughly three dozen short zigzags for about 1,500 ft in the first two miles, then breaks out of the trees and contours east across open slopes to the pass at 3.7 miles. Graded and obvious the whole way.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: High camp used as the base for the north-side approach; permit required, exposed site with no reliable shelter from weather.
waypoints.directions: Turn north (left) at the pass onto the Sahale Arm path, which switchbacks steeply out of the pass at first. About 0.8 mile up, a signed split sends the right-hand branch down to Doubtful Lake; stay left. Above that the path follows the crest of the arm and steepens near the top, where the tread fades into moraine boulders marked by cairns. Roughly 2.2 miles from the pass.

waypoints.name: Sahale-Boston col
waypoints.note: Skirt the top of Sahale and cross this saddle (a small 2-person bivy exists here) onto exposed third-class choss en route toward Boston Peak.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and work up the Sahale Glacier toward the summit pyramid, bearing right onto the gentlest part of the upper slope, then climb over or skirt the summit block and drop down the far side to the saddle. This is where the standard Boston Basin approach joins, having come up the Quien Sabe Glacier from high camp.

waypoints.name: Buckner Mountain (southwest summit)
waypoints.note: Face climb tops out on the summit ridge just below the true summit; upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward to finish.
waypoints.directions: About 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, typically 8-13 pitches and mostly belayed, though strong parties solo it when the face is in good nick. Climb straight up the centre of the lower face until the upper cliffs cut it off, then take several pitches of rising traverse leftward. Within roughly 200 ft of the top, go left around a craggy outcrop at the end of those cliffs before cutting back right to finish. The face is wind-scoured in places and conditions swing between hard scoured ice and moderate powder, so judge it before committing to climbing unroped.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, leave SR-20 onto Cascade River Road (FR-15) and drive to milepost 22.5, where a small pullout is on the left opposite Johannesburg Mountain. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is rough gravel; the road can close at the Eldorado parking area at milepost 20.

approach_variants.name: Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin to the cowskull snowfield
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road. The maintained Cascade Pass trail switchbacks through old growth and traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at 5,400 ft, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft. From the pass take the Sahale Arm trail north through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier and Sahale Glacier Camp near 7,600 ft — 5.9 miles and about 3,940 ft from the trailhead, and the standard base. NPS permit and bear canister required; camp only in the designated sites. Sahale Arm above the meadows is dry, so carry water or a filter.

From camp the route goes off-trail and downhill first: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then a short class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft, and traverse roughly two miles across Horseshoe Basin on talus, slabs and lingering snow, passing near the old Davenport Mine around 7,000 ft, to reach the base of the southwest face.

Most parties take two to three days for the roughly 20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
hazards: A steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be downclimbed, exposed and fall-prone on firm early-season snow
Rockfall across the Horseshoe Basin traverse, which is loose and easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands below the basin ledge system — stay on the mid-elevation line rather than dropping
Steep snow on the cowskull with wet-slide potential in the afternoon; many parties run a picket belay
Loose scree and rubble above the snow, all the way to the summit ridge
An axe and crampons needed for steep snow patches into midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route has a landmark you cannot mistake for anything else, and it is the reason this face is navigable at all: a distinctive cowskull-shaped snowfield high on the face. Climbers describe it as looking like a ghost early in the season. Steepening southwest-facing snowfields lead to a snow chute and then to the cowskull itself, and if you cannot pick a cowskull out of the snow above you, you are under the wrong part of the face.

The mid-approach checkpoint is the Davenport Mine, around 7,000 ft, roughly midway across the Horseshoe Basin traverse. The ruins are unambiguous. If you have crossed the basin without passing old mine workings, you are on the wrong ledge line — and the ones below cliff out.

And the approach begins by losing height, which is the first sanity check of the day: from Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 ft you descend Sahale's south ridge and a class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft before you traverse. If you have been climbing since camp, you have not started the route yet.

Above the cowskull, the ground changes character and that is the signal to put the crampons away: step off the snow, then grovel up loose scree and rubble to the summit ridge, finishing with about 100 ft of class 2-3 rock. Snow the whole way to the top is not this route.

Know which summit you are aiming for: Buckner has two nearly equal tops, the southwest at about 9,114 ft and the northeast about two feet lower, separated by a few hundred feet of ridge. This route reaches the southwest one, which is the accepted high point; the northeast top needs the connecting ridge.

The negative test against the north face is the whole mountain: that route comes from Boston Basin, over Sharkfin Col and across the Boston Glacier, on the opposite side. If you rappelled off a col onto a glacier this morning, you are on the north side.

road.status: Gravel, summer-passable

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15), ~23 mi from Marblemount; self-issue wilderness permit required for overnight camping beyond here.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), roughly 23 miles from Marblemount and about 3,600 feet in elevation. Any overnight camping beyond the trailhead requires a self-issue wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and splits; leave the Pacific Crest/Stehekin trail here and climb north on the Sahale Arm climbers' path toward Sahale Glacier Camp.
waypoints.directions: Well-graded switchbacks through old-growth forest, then a traverse across subalpine meadows to the pass — roughly 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft of gain, and the easiest ground on the whole route.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Established high-camp platforms on the glacier moraine; NPS permit and bear canister required, no campfires, and it's fully exposed to wind and afternoon thunderstorms.
waypoints.directions: Turn north and climber's-right onto the Sahale Arm trail and climb steadily through heather meadow, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier. The upper switchbacks and the final scramble into camp are the steepest walking of the approach. The Arm is dry above the meadows, so this is a leg to carry water up rather than expect to find it.

waypoints.name: Sahale-Buckner notch
waypoints.note: Steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be down-climbed frontpointing to drop into Horseshoe Basin; firm snow makes this exposed and fall-prone in early season.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp heading south onto Sahale's south ridge and descend it on snow and easy class 1-2 rock, working either side of the crest as it steepens. A short class 3 face is downclimbed to reach the notch. The same step has to be reclimbed on the way back, so note the line you take down it.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin traverse (Davenport Mine)
waypoints.note: Broad snow bench traverse of roughly 2 miles across the basin passing the ruins of the historic Davenport silver mine; stay on the mid-elevation ledge system to avoid cliffing out.
waypoints.directions: Downclimb the snow-filled cleft below the notch — parties commonly stay in the moat at its edge until forced onto the snow finger, then front-point down to the bench beneath. From the bench traverse across the basin, holding 6,600 to 6,800 ft beneath Ripsaw Ridge for the first mile, then angling up toward the mine ruins. Rockfall crosses this traverse and the snow softens quickly after mid-morning, so it wants doing early.

waypoints.name: Cowskull snowfield / summit couloir
waypoints.note: Steep snow chute leading to a distinctive cowskull-shaped snow patch used as the navigation cue for the final approach; watch for wet slide potential in the afternoon.
waypoints.directions: From the mine keep angling up across steepening southwest-face snowfields, trending more easterly as you come in under the cowskull, then head straight up the snow chute below it. The angle on this section is enough that many parties put in a running belay on pickets rather than solo it.

waypoints.name: Buckner Mountain (southwest summit)
waypoints.note: True summit reached via loose scree/rubble and a final Class 2-3 rock scramble along the summit ridge.
waypoints.directions: Step off the top of the cowskull, take the crampons off, and grovel up loose scree and rubble to gain the south ridge near 8,800 ft. About a hundred feet of class 2-3 rock along the crest finishes it. All of this last section is loose, so keep the party tight or well out of each other's fall line.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing in high water; cable car or ford
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
Steep brushy timber, slide alder and a loose divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir below the wall
Deep moat at the toe of the buttress late season
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Remote and committing, several days from help
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. The alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is shorter, but the cross-border stretch can be heavy bushwhacking, so the long trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: International border crossing on foot
Overgrown, unmaintained tread; heavy bushwhacking on the cross-border stretch
Same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall below the buttress
Loose blocks on the mid-route traverse; sparse protection on several pitches
Cross-border rescue complications; remote and committing
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Normally the shortest way in, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

road.name: Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32), off the Mount Baker Highway
road.status: Gravel forest road to the trailhead at its end, about 3,100 ft
road.driveNote: From the Mount Baker Highway near Glacier, take Hannegan Pass Road to its end; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the trailhead, and a long multi-day walk over Hannegan Pass follows.
road.seasonalGate: Typically opens after snowmelt in late spring/early summer and closes with the return of snow in fall

waypoints.name: Hannegan Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Bellingham, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east to Glacier and continue about 12.5 miles past the Glacier Public Service Center, then turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FS Road 32) and follow it about 5.3 miles to the road end at about 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park, and overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Bear Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: Climb Trail #674 to Hannegan Pass, drop east into the Chilliwack valley, bear right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail and follow it across the river and down-valley to Bear Creek. Ford Bear Creek, climb brushy timber east to meadows above Ruta Lake and traverse the divide to the 6,480 ft saddle camp. Drop down scree to the glacier remnant, tie in at the buttress toe, climb the 21 pitches, then scramble right to the summit ridge.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Mount Baker Highway (SR-542), about 12.5 miles east of the Glacier Public Service Center, turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32) and drive about 5.3 miles to the road-end trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Same gully as the standard buttress — the difference is one turn at its top
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Southwest Buttress's, without exception: from the Cascade River Road trailhead near 2,100 ft, cross the river, climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado / Roush Creek Basin, and on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — about 5.8 miles and 5,500 ft from the car.

From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (the best passage is on its skier's right side near the steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent, often snow-filled gully that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress. A rope may be wanted here: a moat guarding the base can present an exposed, deep gap.

Everything to this point is shared with the 1985 standard line. The two routes part company at the top of the gully, and after two pitches they rejoin.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, when the approach glaciers are consolidated and the buttress is snow-free
hazards: Crevasse and moat crossings on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
A long, remote approach with no easy bail once you are on the buttress
Sustained 5.10 low on the route, which is the wrong place to discover the crux pitch is wet
Loose rock on the upper pitches once the two routes have rejoined
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The two routes share every step of the approach and separate at one point: the top of the snow gully. The standard Southwest Buttress traverses around to the right there. This route goes straight up.

And then the confirmation is countable, which is as good as this gets on an alpine route: two direct-start pitches of fourth and low-fifth scrambling lead to three vertical cracks. You climb the rightmost of the three. Not the left, not the middle — the rightmost, which starts around 5.8, turns strenuous at 5.10, and finishes with a mantel onto a large bench.

So the test is: count to three, take the right-hand one, and expect a mantel. If there are not three cracks in front of you, you have gone right at the top of the gully and you are on the standard line — a fine route, two grades easier, and the one you will end up on anyway.

The second pitch is the other half of the answer: awkward 5.8+ climbing rejoins the original 1985 route at a large white slabby rock. That white slab is the merge point and it is named in the route's own description. Once you are past it, the two lines are one and the remaining pitches to the summit ridge are the standard route's.

So the direct start is two pitches long. If you are three or four pitches in and still looking for the merge, you have missed the white slab — the merge is early, not high.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel the rest of the way; the Eldorado Creek trailhead is at about mile 20 and the road continues to the Cascade Pass trailhead. NPS listed the road as open on its road-conditions page as of 3 July 2026 and no longer lists the June 2026 vehicle closure at Eldorado Creek. Washouts and landslides have closed this road at Eldorado Creek repeatedly over the years, so check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
road.driveNote: Not suitable for low-clearance vehicles beyond the pavement; vehicles/trailers over 22 ft or 8 ft wide prohibited beyond mile 18.
road.seasonalGate: Typically snow-gated in winter/spring; usually opens to Cascade Pass trailhead by late June in a normal year.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the standard Southwest Buttress; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River and follow the Cascade River Road about 20 miles, gravel for the second half, to the small Eldorado trailhead lot on the right near milepost 20, about 2,100 ft. Overnight stays need a North Cascades backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf shared with the standard Southwest Buttress route.
waypoints.directions: From the lot, walk about 90 feet back down the road and look for the log or clump of trees spanning the river; cross there, then head roughly 100 feet away from the water to pick up the climbers' path and turn upstream on it. The path climbs steeply through forest and talus into Eldorado Basin and on up to the Inspiration Glacier shelf, about 5,500 ft of gain to camps near 7,400-7,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Crossing point from Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier, shared with the standard buttress approach.
waypoints.directions: Rope up at camp and cross the Inspiration Glacier northeast to the low point on the divide. The ground is otherwise gentle; crevasses are the only real difficulty.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Shared approach point; the Direct variant leaves the standard line at the top of the approach gully, going straight up where the standard route traverses right.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the col onto the McAllister Glacier and work down and across it, keeping to its skier's right where the ice steepens and breaks up, then traverse toward the pass.

waypoints.name: Direct Southwest Buttress topout
waypoints.note: Harder direct start (5.10a) rejoins the standard buttress line before the final corner to the summit ridge.
waypoints.directions: About 700 vertical feet below the pass, start up the prominent gully running to the base of the buttress; it usually holds snow year-round. Rope up before its top, because the moat guarding the base of the rock can open into a deep, exposed gap. From the gully exit do not traverse right onto the standard 1985 line: carry straight on up two direct pitches of 4th and low-5th scrambling to three vertical cracks, take the rightmost at about 5.8 into the strenuous 5.10 crux and mantel onto a large bench, then follow awkward 5.8+ ground toward the large white slabby rock where the original route comes back in.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: True summit shared with the standard Southwest Buttress finish.
waypoints.directions: From the junction with the 1985 line, blocky mid-5th rock and a final corner lead onto the summit ridge, then a short scramble along it gains the true summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)

approach_variants.name: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,100 ft — the first ten miles paved, the rest rough gravel and high-clearance recommended. Hike the Eldorado climbers' trail through forest, cross the creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft, roughly four miles and 6,000 ft of gain.

From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle at about 7,600 ft. That col is the base.

Most parties take eight to twelve hours round trip from high camp, and descend by the Northwest Ridge rather than reversing this line — which means the day ends on unfamiliar ground with rappels and a moat, so scout the Northwest Ridge's top as you pass it.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once glacier bridges and moats have stabilised but before the early-season storms return
hazards: Crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
Loose, thinly protectable rock on the first pitch off the col — test every placement
A bottomless moat on the glacier traverse partway up the route, where the line steps off the ridge and back on
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a named col: the one between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle, at about 7,600 ft. The climbing starts immediately off it — steep, exposed mid-fifth moves straight from the col, no walk-in. If you had to travel further along the glacier after crossing a col before you found rock, you are at the wrong col.

The first pitch identifies itself by being nasty and by carrying a marker: it is a loose, poorly protectable 5.5, and A horn with an existing sling sits about 100 ft up. Loose rock plus a slung horn a rope-length up is the confirmation.

There is an alternative start and it has its own landmark: a line beneath the 'cannonball hole' to the right avoids that first loose section, at the cost of a moat crossing. A hole in the rock you could name is not a feature you find by accident — if you can see it, you are in the right place and you have a choice to make.

Tell it from its neighbours by length and by difficulty, because all four routes on this needle are different sizes. This one is longer and a bit harder than the Northwest Ridge (three short pitches from a small col at the top of the McAllister apron) and easier than the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from a gully 700 ft below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass). It follows the centre portion of the rock on an obvious ridge line.

The route steps off the ridge partway up and that is expected, not an error: after several ropelengths of class 3-4 you descend into a notch, traverse the glacier, and regain the ridge at a ledge marked by quartzite bands. Watch for a bottomless moat there. Pale banded rock on a ledge is the marker to aim for.

And the finish is countable: two short rappels drop into the notch below the true summit, then two sustained 5.7 crack pitches to the top. If you have climbed one hard pitch and stood on a summit, you were on the sub-summit tower.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Seasonal gravel/paved mountain road; typically opens by late June and can be delayed to early July by snow or storm damage; subject to periodic closures at various mileposts for washouts, maintenance, or emergencies (e.g. wildfire) — check current NPS road conditions before driving
road.driveNote: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado Trailhead parking area (~2,100 ft). The first 10 miles are paved; miles 10-20 are rough gravel; the final few miles are narrow with steep drop-offs and washouts requiring a high-clearance vehicle. No trailers or vehicles over 22 ft long/8 ft wide are allowed past milepost 18.
road.seasonalGate: Winter/off-season gate; road access to the Eldorado Trailhead area (near MP 20) is closed outside the open season

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado Creek trailhead, near 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved and the remainder is rough gravel, so high clearance is recommended. Park in the roadside lot at mile 20; from there the walking starts by crossing the North Fork Cascade River on logs and picking up the steep climbers' path beside Eldorado Creek.

waypoints.name: Col between Pt. 8386 and Dorado Needle (East Ridge start)
waypoints.directions: Cross the river on logs and climb the steep climbers' path beside Eldorado Creek, then the boulder fields and the Eldorado Glacier to the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak and the high camps near 7,400 ft, roughly 4 miles and 6,000 ft of gain. From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to the col between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle, about 7,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.directions: Climb straight off the col on loose, thin first-pitch rock (a slung horn sits about 100 ft up), then several ropelengths along the ridge. Drop into a notch, traverse the glacier to a ledge with pale quartzite bands (watch the moat) and regain the ridge to the sub-summit tower. Two short rappels reach the notch below the summit, then two 5.7 crack pitches lead to the top.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
approach_variants.hours: 5-7 to high camp, 3-5 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
hazards: Cascade River log crossing — slick when wet, position shifts year to year
Boulder field is the crux of the walk, worse descending under a heavy pack
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, worsening as the day warms
Featureless flat glacier — whiteout navigation to The Gap
Exposed summit knife-edge; crevasses on the ridge crest itself
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start on this route — the climbing is the summit snow arete, and finding it means finding one gap on an otherwise featureless glacier.

From high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle the Inspiration Glacier runs away nearly flat to the west. Cross it aiming for the obvious low gap in Eldorado's lower East Ridge, universally called 'The Gap'. Once you have stepped through the gap you are on the East Ridge; before that you are still on flat glacier.

The confirmation underfoot is that the ground stops being flat and becomes a defined crest, with glacier falling away on both sides rather than one. From the gap, go a short way further up onto the snow until a distinct ramp leads leftward/rightward onto the ridge crest proper — parties consistently report a gentle ramp reaching the base of the knife edge from its far right side. That ramp, and the point where the crest narrows so that both sides drop, is the base of the climbing.

The common error is stopping short: the flat Inspiration is genuinely disorienting in cloud, parties describe an hour of whiteout walking to reach the gap, and parties drift too low into crevassed glacier instead of holding the line to the low point on the skyline. Take and hold a bearing from camp. Later in the season the crest melts out and parties move onto the steeper snow slope to the right of the bare ridge, where crevasses open — early season the same crest can be broad enough to skin.

Stay roped on the ridge. It is not a rock ridge you have escaped the glacier onto; the line travels back onto glacier and crevasses exist on the crest itself.

approach_variants.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
approach_variants.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.
approach_variants.season: late May-June
hazards: Avalanche paths across the approach and the road in spring
Snow-bridged creek channels in the lower basins — parties have punched through
Road may be closed or buried well below the trailhead
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Late May and June, when snow covers the upper approach and the boulder field, and parties accept avalanche exposure for faster ground; ski parties also choose it for the descent.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same gap in the lower East Ridge, but early season it is broader and more forgiving: the ridge is wide, sometimes wide enough to skin, and the knife edge that defines the route later in the summer may not have formed yet. Do not treat a wide, easy crest as evidence you are in the wrong place — the landmark is still The Gap, the low point on the ridge skyline reached by crossing the flat Inspiration.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Seasonally open, roughly late June through fall; paved miles 0-10 from SR-20 at Marblemount, rough/washboard gravel miles 10-20, prone to ruts and washouts
road.driveNote: Eldorado trailhead parking (with pit toilet) is at mile 20; vehicles/trailers over 22 ft long or 8 ft wide are prohibited past milepost 18.
road.seasonalGate: Closed by snow in winter; opening date varies year to year and can slip into July

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount for about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead pullout, about 3 miles short of the road's end at Cascade Pass, roughly 2,100 feet; the first ten miles are paved and the rest is gravel and washboard. There's a pit toilet at the parking area. The road typically doesn't open until late May or June, depending on snowpack. Camping here needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit reserved in advance, but the permit itself must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center before you drive up.

waypoints.name: Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp
waypoints.directions: Walk about 90 ft back down the road and cross the Cascade River on the log, then go about 100 ft straight away from the river to the climbers' path. It climbs steeply through timber for about 1,500 ft to a boulder field; follow cairns up it, staying climber's right of Eldorado Creek, into Eldorado Creek Basin. Cross the ridge at about 6,100 ft into Roush Basin, take talus and slabs onto the Eldorado Glacier, rope up, and climb it to camp near 7,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Inspiration Glacier
waypoints.directions: Roped, cross the nearly flat Inspiration Glacier toward the obvious low gap near the east end of Eldorado's East Ridge. Take a bearing from camp, because the glacier is featureless in cloud. Pass north through the gap onto the glacier slopes north of the ridge.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb west up the glacier slopes north of the ridge, keeping the crest on your left and probing suspect snow bridges, to where the slope steepens below the knife-edge. Follow the narrow, often corniced snow crest to the small summit. An axe and crampons are essential, and many parties place pickets along the crest.

approach_variants.name: Rappel off the ice cap into the Marble Creek cirque, then the couloir splitting the northwest face
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the mountain's northwest side and the wild Marble Creek Cirque. High camp is either in Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek Basin or at the Eldorado-Inspiration site near 7,500-7,600 ft.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch sometimes called the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and rappel from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.
approach_variants.season: Highly conditions-dependent. Spring, roughly April to early May, can give steep thin ice and moderate mixed; mid-to-late summer the couloir is usually mostly snow with a few ice steps; a good cold snap in late October or November can bring in firm, well-bonded ice. Grade moves with it, roughly AI2-3 up to WI3 in lean conditions
hazards: An extreme funnel: the whole face feeds into a narrow confined couloir, so anything the leader dislodges lands on the belay
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers and a long featureless crossing that is disorienting in whiteout
A moat or bergschrund where the glacier meets the couloir, widening through the summer
Cornices and crevasses at the couloir's exit near the knife-edge ridge
Rappelling the couloir is the only retreat once you are high, and it is slow — the practical escape is over the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Once you are in the cirque the route is obvious, and two separate parties say so in nearly the same words: on looking up from below the rappel, one recorded instantly seeing the line — steep, fat and unmistakable. The couloir splits the northwest face and there is nothing else in the cirque it could be confused with. So the navigation problem is not identifying the couloir; it is getting into the cirque at all.

The notch is the thing to find, and it is shared with the North Ridge. It is the obvious gap between the North Ridge and the First Rock Spire, at about 8,100 ft, reached by traversing north from the East Ridge glacier track. At that notch the two routes go opposite ways: rappel down the far side into the cirque and you are on this route; climb steep snow up onto the rock crest and you are on the North Ridge.

The base itself is the transition at about 7,800 ft where the couloir meets the glacier — which is the usual place to find the moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier before you reach it.

One branch point worth knowing: at least one party climbed a steep line just to climber's left of the main gut of the couloir rather than the gut itself. Both go; the gut is the route as described.

Confirm on the climbing: the line runs from about 7,800 ft to about 8,800 ft, roughly 1,000 ft, usually two or three long pitches or simul-climbed blocks, and the character is a succession of short ice steps broken by lower-angle snow rather than one continuous wall. Steps around 70-80 degrees with occasional near-vertical bulges for a body length is right; sustained vertical ice for a full pitch is not this route in any season.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead pullout at about mile 20, at roughly 2,100 feet. The road usually doesn't open until late May or June, depending on snowpack. waypoints.name: Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp
waypoints.directions: Walk about 90 ft back down the road and cross the Cascade River on the log, then go about 100 ft straight away from the river to the climbers' path. It climbs steeply through timber for about 1,500 ft to a boulder field; follow cairns up it, staying climber's right of Eldorado Creek, into Eldorado Creek Basin. Cross the ridge at about 6,100 ft into Roush Basin, take talus and slabs onto the Eldorado Glacier, rope up, and climb it to camp near 7,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Base of northwest couloir
waypoints.directions: Roped, cross the glacier past the East Ridge and head for the obvious notch between Eldorado's North Ridge and the first rock spire (Dean's Tower), at about 8,100 ft. Rappel from the piton anchor on the far side into the Marble Creek cirque (one 60 m rope does it), then traverse a few hundred feet across the small glacier to the foot of the couloir near 7,800 ft. A moat or bergschrund there widens through the summer.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the couloir that splits the northwest face, about 1,000 ft of short ice steps separated by lower-angle snow, to a small flat area just below the summit ridge. From there follow the exposed snow knife-edge to the summit.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: Cross the Cascade River on the log and climb the climbers' path and boulder field into Eldorado Creek Basin, then go over the ridge into Roush Basin and up the Eldorado Glacier. approach_variants.name: Over the ice cap to Dorado Needle Col, then down into Marble Creek Cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, and gain the Eldorado Glacier. Most parties treat this as three days: approach, climb, exit, with a base camp at the East Ridge site near 7,500 ft or on the western margin of the Eldorado Glacier.

The defining feature of the approach is that you must get down to the base. The line runs from the ice cap across to the Dorado Needle Col area, then a loose fourth-class downclimb — accounts on the neighbouring line describe rappelling, steep névé downclimbing and moat work over roughly 1,000 ft of descent — into the Marble Creek Cirque on Eldorado's west side, and the toe of the ridge is at the bottom of that.

This is a long day: parties have taken up to about 17 hours round trip from the East Ridge base camp, and an unplanned bivouac is a real possibility if the middle section goes slowly.

A warning from parties who have done it: published route descriptions for this arête have been called inaccurate and sandbagged, and at least one party went off route immediately as a result. Trust the terrain over the topo.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer once fully snow-free, with maximum daylight for a long climbing day; Cascade River Road is often not open until late June
hazards: A loose fourth-class downclimb into the cirque that has to be reversed or bypassed at the end of the day
Rockfall and loose rock over the full length of the arête, including the opening pitch
Large moats on both sides of the ridge at its foot, and a building-sized snow remnant to keep clear of
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers that open through the summer
A confusing middle section where slow progress turns into a bivouac
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive at this route by going down, not up, and that is the first check. The toe of the arête sits at roughly 6,000 ft in the Marble Creek Cirque, reached only by a loose fourth-class downclimb off the Dorado Needle Col area. If your approach has been a continuous ascent from camp, you have not reached this route.

The sequence at the bottom is countable and it is the positive test: from the snow at the base, spooky scrambling on glacier-polished slabs leads to a steep, open chimney feature. Slabs first, chimney second. The rock climbing proper begins a couple of hundred feet above the toe of the ridge on its north side.

The first pitch confirms it by being bad. The opening pitch is unbelievably loose 5.6 on the ridge crest. If your first pitch is clean and solid, you are on the wrong feature.

There is a harder line on the same wall and it is worth knowing before you commit: the southwest arête — climbed in full only in 2022, about 3,600 ft at grade V 5.10 — takes the same cirque approach and a different arête. This route is the shorter 1969 line at about 2,800 ft, sustained 5.6-5.7 with an old-school 5.8 crux. If the climbing is relentlessly harder than mid-fifth from low down, you are on the wrong arête.

Confirm at the crux: a set of rocky towers ends in a face traverse protected by a single in-situ piton. One piton, one traverse. That is the hardest move on the route and it is the landmark for the upper half.
