waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak
waypoints.directions: Cross the Cascade River on logs a short way downstream of the parking and follow the steep climbers' trail up beside Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin and onto the Eldorado Glacier. approach_variants.name: East around the basin and up the loose gullies to the notch below the Solitary Gendarme
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and Boston Basin climbers' trail as the West Ridge — the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about a mile, then a steep path with several creek crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft, then talus and heather to the usual high camp at 6,300-6,600 ft, roughly four to five miles and three to four hours from the car.

From camp, do NOT cross toward the south-face couloir. Traverse climber's-left and east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies flanking the glacier on Forbidden's east side, sometimes loosely called the Unnamed Glacier. This leg is the honest part of the route's reputation: a few hours over choss-covered slabs, loose rock and seepage, several small stream crossings, and usually a snow gully at the end that wants crampons or microspikes to gain the upper benches. Parties describe holding a bearing of roughly 058 degrees up the east side of that glacier.

Reckon five to six hours and over 5,000 ft above the trailhead to the notch — noticeably longer and far more route-finding than reaching the West Ridge notch.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; August is the most reliable for dry granite
hazards: Hours of loose, choss-covered slabs and seepage on the approach, with real route-finding in poor visibility
A snow gully at the top of the approach that wants crampons even in midsummer
Aging fixed rappel anchors in the gendarme notches
Sustained exposure and complex route-finding over multiple gendarmes once on the crest
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long crest with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark is a single tower with a name: the solitary gendarme. The high bivy sits at roughly 8,000 ft, about 300 ft below it, and the notch where the technical climbing starts is just above that bivy. A lone tower standing up on the crest, with the ridge running away west toward the summit, is the confirmation you are at the right place on a ridge that offers many wrong ones.

Why that matters more here than elsewhere: this crest carries several gendarmes and the ridge can be joined almost anywhere along it. Joining it high — past the gendarmes, with an unobstructed view of the summit and nothing in the way — means you have missed the route rather than found a shortcut. If there is nothing between you and the summit, you are too high.

The first move test: from the notch you go left around the first gendarme, then simul-climb easy blocks at about 5.4 on clean granite to gain the crest proper. Easy ground first, hard ground later. If your opening pitch is hard, you are not on the East Ridge Direct.

The direct line is defined by refusing the bypasses. Every gendarme here can be walked around on the north or south flank. A day that never once required a move you would rope up for means you have been taking the bypasses and are on the easier variant, not the Direct.

Confirm at the crux, late: the 5.8 crux comes after climbing a steep pitch up the last gendarme and rappelling down its back side into a narrow notch with a steep wall directly ahead. A notch you scrambled into rather than rappelled into is not that notch.

Do not confuse this ridge with the east ledges. The Ledges are the loose descent traverse that stays well below the crest and rejoins the ridge near the Solitary Gendarme. If you are traversing ledges rather than climbing a crest, you are on the descent line — the one that carries a documented fatality.

Expect pavement for roughly the first 10 miles and rough gravel after that. The park bars trailers past its boundary at mile 18 and any vehicle over 22 ft long or 8 ft wide, and advises against sedans and low-clearance cars.
road.seasonalGate: In a normal year the road is open through to the Cascade Pass trailhead by the end of June (early July after a big snow year or storm damage); outside that season the park may gate it at different points for winter, maintenance or emergencies.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road ~21.7 mi from Marblemount; NW Forest Pass to park, overnight stays need a park backcountry permit, picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Marblemount, turn onto the Cascade River Road, which crosses the Skagit River and runs east, paved for about 10 miles and then rough gravel. Drive about 22 miles to a small pullout on the left beneath the northeast face of Johannesburg Mountain, at about 3,200 ft, with room for only a handful of cars. The road usually opens to its end by late June or early July. Overnight stays in the park require a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin
waypoints.directions: Follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about a mile and watch for the climbers' path leaving it. The path climbs steeply through forest with several creek crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft, then over talus and heather to the camps in Boston Basin.

waypoints.name: East end of ridge
waypoints.directions: From camp, do not head toward the south-face couloir; traverse east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies along the east side of the glacier below Forbidden. Expect hours of loose, choss-covered slabs, seepage and small stream crossings, usually finishing with a snow gully that wants crampons, then broken rock and snow up to the notch just above the high bivy, below the solitary gendarme.

waypoints.name: Forbidden Peak summit
waypoints.directions: From the notch, go left around the first gendarme and simul-climb easy blocks to the crest, then follow it west over the gendarmes rather than taking their bypasses. Rappel off the back of the last gendarme into a narrow notch, climb the 5.8 crux crack on the wall ahead, and continue on easier ground to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Off the Bridge Creek trail to the toe of the arete descending northeast off the main ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass at about 4,400 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

About two miles up it, leave the trail at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek and bushwhack steeply through slide alder and timber to the toe of the arete. Carrying on past Grizzly Creek to the ford and the slabs beside the waterfall leads to the Goode Glacier and the Northeast Buttress, not to this ridge.

The total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.
approach_variants.season: Late summer, August into September, once the approach bushwhack and the glacier are most passable; a long committing route that wants a stable weather window
hazards: Hidden cliff bands inside the brush
A very long sustained ridge — 2,800 to 3,000 ft of climbing with about 5,000 ft of exposure on one side and 4,000 on the other
Mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches, so long sections carry limited protection
Very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are both thin
Benightment on the ridge is a real risk, and the standard descent drops into the Park Creek drainage on the far side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The feature is a clean-looking arete that descends northeast off the main ridge, and you aim for its toe. It sits close beneath the Goode Glacier's lower icefall — near it, not on it.

The single strongest test is that you never cross the glacier. The Northeast Buttress, the peak's other big route on this side, is reached by stepping off the Goode Glacier across a moat at a band of red rock. This route is gained from the east, from brush and rock, with no glacier crossing at all. If you have crampons on to reach your base, you are on the Buttress.

The arete announces itself by being clean. It is described as a clean-looking arete precisely because the ground around it is not — the last half mile of approach is slide alder and timber. Emerging from brush onto a distinct clean crest running down to the northeast is the confirmation.

Count the first stage: simul-climbing up the lower arete to a tower at about 8,200 ft, then one rappel off it, and only then running-belay climbing along the crest toward the southeast peak. A rappel early on a ridge you are ascending is a strong positional marker and it is the first one this route gives you.

The crux is late and it is above the glacier: three long pitches of 5.9-5.10 on the southeast peak headwall, with easier options further left, and then an overhanging 5.10 headwall above the Goode Glacier near Black Tooth Notch with an icy moat to negotiate. If you have met your hardest climbing in the first half of the day, you are on something else.

approach_variants.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,400 ft), just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The entry is marked: a narrow ledge with a cairn on it leads into the southwest gully. After skirting snow you scramble talus and loose scree to that ledge. A cairn on a narrow ledge is the confirmation; an unmarked scramble straight into a gully is not this route.

Inside the gully the test is colour, and it is both a route-finding and a safety instruction: hug the left side, where the dark rock is solid. Parties call that band the black stairs and it offers cleaner scrambling than the middle of the gully. If you are on pale, rubbly rock, you are in the gut of the couloir and on the loose line.

Expect one short low-fifth pitch low down, then class 3 and 4 in the main gully, steepening near the notch between the summit and the West Tower.

Black Tooth Notch is the upper landmark and it is shared, so it identifies the mountain rather than the route: a foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse, with a fixed sling marking the crux step, and loose rock throughout. The Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge both descend through it; this is the only one of the three that climbs up through it.

And the most useful negative fact is about going down, because that is when it bites: the couloir's mouth opens onto cliffs above a waterfall. Exit left onto easier heather benches rather than continuing straight down. A party that is still descending the fall line when it hears water below has gone too far.

waypoints.note: Leave the Pacific Crest Trail here and turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail toward Goode's north side.
waypoints.directions: Cross SR-20 on the connector trail and hike the Pacific Crest Trail south along Bridge Creek, losing elevation steadily through forest for about 9.5 miles to the North Fork Camp junction. Turn off the PCT here onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail.

waypoints.name: Grizzly Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Usually an easy log crossing but reported as a dangerously high, hard-to-find ford in early season; trail turns brushy/overgrown just beyond it.
waypoints.directions: Head upstream on the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail to the Grizzly Creek crossing, usually an easy log but a high, hard-to-find ford in early season.

waypoints.name: Lateral moraine camp above Goode Glacier
waypoints.note: Established bivy atop the lateral moraine overlooking the Goode Glacier's seracs; standard base camp for the Southwest Couloir attempt.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the North Fork trail as it grows brushier, then leave the tread and ford the North Fork, easiest a short way upstream near a cairn. Follow an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder tunnels, then climb heather and scree to the lateral moraine above the Goode Glacier.

waypoints.name: Goode Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier from the moraine camp to reach the couloir base; route-finding is tricky and late-season snow bridges can be deteriorated.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp across the moraine and onto the glacier remnant toward the couloir. Route-finding is tricky and late-season snow bridges can be rotten, so rope up.

waypoints.name: Black Tooth Notch
waypoints.note: Foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse (fixed sling marks the crux step); rock here is loose/"garbage" — watch for rockfall onto climbers below.
waypoints.directions: Scramble talus and loose scree to the rotten ridge below the couloir and the narrow cairned ledge that leads into it. Climb the couloir on the solid dark rock of the black stairs along its left side, class 3-4 with a short low fifth-class step low down, to Black Tooth Notch, gained by an exposed class 4 traverse with a fixed sling at the crux step.

waypoints.name: Goode Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Highest point in North Cascades National Park; summit block above the notch adds exposed class 4-5 moves before the true top.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, traverse across the upper Northeast Face and climb the exposed class 4-5 summit block to the true top.

approach_variants.name: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road — the upper gravel section is gated and often does not open until late June or July — follow the well-graded Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low down, so fill up before the switchbacks.

At the pass leave the maintained tread for the climbers' path heading south-southeast, a rising traverse across snow or heather on Mixup Peak's flanks to the base of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft. Ascend moderate glacier and snow slopes to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft. From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock and heather benches to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water in the basin.

From camp the peak is a side trip: up toward the south flank, across a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft, then broken granite slabs to the ridge. About a mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly an hour to an hour and a half for a fit party.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July and wants an axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free
hazards: Crevasses and snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
Icy, steep snow on the Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake descent, worse refrozen in the early morning or late in the day
A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft that wants an axe and crampons even mid-summer
Loose rock and multiple similar-looking gully lines on the granite benches — the main route-finding crux
Short but exposed moves along the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Kool-Aid Lake, and above it the climb is route-finding rather than following a line. On the way up, the steep snow band around 7,100 ft is the position check: it sits between camp and the granite, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 2-3 scramble. Beyond it, broken granite leads to a gully that gains the summit ridge. Several similar-looking gullies lead up; parties report that more than one of them goes, so pick the cleanest and keep checking that it tops out on the ridge. On the ridge you reach a false summit first. The true top is a short way beyond it along the ridge, so do not turn around on the first high point. And do not confuse the basin with Cache Col. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier; Kool-Aid Lake is about a mile beyond it and a descent below it. The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a description of S Mountain is describing this same summit.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15), 23.1 mi from Marblemount; day use is free but overnight parties need a North Cascades NP backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: Cascade River Road runs roughly 23 miles from Marblemount, pavement giving way to gravel for the upper half. The last gravel section is gated through the winter and typically does not open until the snow clears, often not until late June or July, so confirm the road is open all the way to the end before committing to the drive.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail; camping is prohibited at the pass itself, so continue toward Pelton Basin or contour east/south toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Follow the well-graded, heavily used Cascade Pass Trail about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to the pass. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so fill bottles before starting the switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Cache Col / Cache Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rocky gap between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak at the head of Cache Glacier; cross the glacier here and watch for open crevasses in low-snow late-season conditions.
waypoints.directions: Climb back west to the Cascade Pass area and leave the maintained tread on the climbers' boot track heading south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over loose ground, heather and firm morning snow patches across Mixup Peak's flanks to the toe of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft, then up moderate snow slopes to the notch. Crevasses open here by late summer, so carry a rope and crevasse-rescue kit and be ready to use them.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine tarn ~1 mile SSE of Cache Col that serves as the standard day-1 camp for parties climbing Hurry-up Peak or starting the Ptarmigan Traverse; often still snow/ice-covered into August.
waypoints.directions: From the col drop and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock, heather benches and occasional snowfields to the tarn. It is the only dependable water in the basin and can still be partly frozen early in the season.

waypoints.name: Exposed summit ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scrambling with moderate exposure along the final summit ridge; early-season parties report steep snow here that warrants pickets for protection.
waypoints.directions: From the lake climb south, over scree, heather and broken granite benches, then take a gully up to the summit ridge. A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft commonly persists into midsummer, so carry an axe and crampons even in August. Route-finding on the benches is the real crux here: several similar-looking gully lines lead up and not all of them are the right one.

waypoints.name: Hurry-up Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (historically also called Ess/S Mountain); open view north to Trapper Lake and the rest of the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks.
waypoints.directions: Once on the summit ridge, follow it past a false summit to the true top, which lies a short way beyond. The scrambling is class 2-3 with moderate exposure, and the rock is loose enough that holds want testing before they are weighted.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the very start, which has washed out
long waterless switchbacks on both trail sections
crevasses and moats on the Jerry Glacier, worse as a bare-ice slip hazard late in the season
fire-damaged forest and unstable ground near Jerry Lakes
loose rock on the face where holds pull off freely - keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked
route-finding for the ramp and hidden chimney, which are hard to relocate on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is found by a slung boulder and a hidden break, not by a bearing. From the Jerry Lakes basin, traverse the heather shelf and go through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,000 to 7,200 ft. This shoulder is the decision point for the whole mountain. For the South Face you now turn west and make a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, often moving in the shallow moat where old snow has pulled away from the rock.

The positive marker is a boulder with sling material on it, standing above the snow patches under the lower cliff band. The break in that band is a left-slanting ramp leading to a short class 4 step and then a hidden class 3 chimney, and it stays invisible until you are almost underneath it. Looking up from a distance and seeing no way through the band is the normal experience and is not evidence you are in the wrong place; looking up and seeing an obvious open gully is evidence that you are, because the break here is not obvious.

If you are climbing the crest of the ridge itself rather than traversing beneath a face, you have stayed on the southeast ridge and are on the other route. The South Face leaves the ridge at the shoulder and does not return to it until well above the cliff band, near 8,600 ft, where a band of scree beside a snow patch delivers you back onto the crest.

A cross-check above the band: 400 to 500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges linked by harder steps, then easier ground. Sustained hard climbing straight off the chimney means you have taken the wrong line through the band.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent. Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of Crater Creek Basin if you camp low
no water above the lakes or the meadows
exposed camps with weather coming over the crest
loose ground on the traverse under the face
approach_variants.whyThisWay: For parties wanting the meadow camp, which keeps running water later in the season and puts summit day on the right side of the notch, at the cost of a descent and re-ascent.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever camp you use, the route starts at the same place: the level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,000 to 7,200 ft. From the lakes you reach it by crossing the notch south of the lakes and climbing back out of Crater Creek Basin; from the meadows camp you climb straight to it.

The shoulder is recognised by being level. The ridge relents here into a flat step before it rears up again, and the ground to the west opens into the scree traverse under the face. If you are still climbing steadily with no let-up, you are below it.

From the shoulder the south face goes west and down-slope of the crest, on scree and dirt, toward snow patches and a slung boulder under a continuous cliff band. If you find yourself scrambling directly up the crest above the shoulder you are on the Southeast Ridge line instead - a legitimate route, but not this one, and it has no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on it.

road.name: State Route 20 / North Cascades Highway
road.status: Seasonal — closed roughly early Dec to mid-April/May between MP134 (Ross Dam TH) and MP171 (Silver Star Gate), sometimes retreating further to Newhalem (MP120) / Early Winters (MP178)
road.driveNote: Canyon Creek Trailhead is on SR-20 about 16 miles west of Rainy Pass (9.5 miles east of the Diablo Lake overlook), roughly 55 miles west of Winthrop.
road.seasonalGate: Gates at Ross Dam TH/Newhalem on the west, Silver Star/Early Winters on the east, per WSDOT plowing progress

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue free Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead register; $5 day-use/Northwest Forest Pass required for the SR-20 lot near Granite/Canyon Creek.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20, roughly 16 miles west of Rainy Pass at about 1,900 feet. The lot takes a $5 day-use fee or a Northwest Forest Pass, and there is a register at the trailhead where you self-issue the free Pasayten Wilderness permit. If you are camping, the high camps fall inside the North Cascades park complex and Ross Lake NRA backcountry, so arrange a wilderness camping permit before you leave. The route is usually climbed August into September.

waypoints.name: Jackita Ridge Trail / Crater Lake Trail fork
waypoints.note: Trail #738 switchbacks ~3,400 ft in 4 miles (about 55 switchbacks) to this fork; leave Jackita Ridge Trail and go left for Crater Lake.
waypoints.directions: Cross Canyon Creek on the log-and-plank crossing right at the start; it can wash out in high water, so check its condition before committing to the trip. Above it the trail settles into roughly fifty switchbacks and about 3,400 ft of forested climbing over four miles. Carry water from the creek, because the hillside above holds none.

waypoints.name: Crater Lake
waypoints.note: Grade flattens around 5,000 ft at the lake basin; campsites sit on the rocky south lip and the outlet is the last reliable water before cross-country travel toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Bear left at the fork and contour about a mile into the lake basin, losing a little height as the grade finally eases — the only downhill on the way in.

waypoints.name: Crater Mountain south saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country ridge-gain point above Crater Lake where the trail ends and the route drops off-trail toward the Jerry Glacier remnant.
waypoints.directions: Pick the trail back up above the lake and grind out roughly 2,200 ft of long, hot, exposed switchbacks with no water on any of them. Somewhere around 6,700-7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse off toward the gap between Crater Mountain's main summit and its east peak. Most parties are a little over four hours from the car when they reach it.

waypoints.name: Jerry Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small crevassed glacier below the saddle; rope up or wear crampons to descend safely toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the route goes downhill onto the ice on the far side. Early in the season the glacier is snow-covered and crevassed enough to justify a rope and crampons; by late summer it is often patchy or nearly bare, which makes the crossing simpler but the consequences of a slide worse.

waypoints.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp
waypoints.note: Established bench camp near Jerry Lakes reached roughly 8-8.5 hrs from the trailhead; standard bivy for a South Face summit push the next morning.
waypoints.directions: Continue down off the ice into the lakes basin, losing around 800 ft over heather, slabs and boulders with no set line to follow. Fill water at the lakes: this is the last of it before the face.

waypoints.name: Hidden chimney / red gully, South Face
waypoints.note: Class-3 hidden chimney cuts the lower cliff band above a fish-shaped snowfield and a slinged rappel boulder; loose rock, a short rappel, and exposed steep snow through here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the heather shelf out of the basin and through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,200 ft. From there make a rising traverse on scree westward beneath the face to the snow patches under its lower cliff band, often moving in the shallow moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock. Those snowfields are steep enough to want crampons late in the season, and the break in the cliff band above them stays hidden until you are almost underneath it.

waypoints.name: Jack Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a notch just west of the summit blocks followed by a short, exposed class-3 finish.
waypoints.directions: Above the cliff band the face gives 400-500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges strung together by harder class 4 steps and traverses, then eases into straightforward scrambling and a band of scree beside a snow patch that returns you to the southeast ridge near 8,600 ft. Traverse and drop slightly to get in under the summit cliffs, then take the partly snow-filled gully above at class 3 and 4 with one step that can feel low fifth. Holds pull off freely on all of it, so keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked in the gully.

access.fees: No National Park entrance fee. Wilderness permit: $10/person + $6 reservation fee if reserved via recreation.gov; free if self-issued at the trailhead.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry wilderness permit required year-round for any overnight stay beyond the trailhead ($10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee if booked ahead on recreation.gov; free self-issue permits available at the trailhead kiosk when the Marblemount office is closed). A separate day-use permit is required for Cascade Pass day hikers June-September but does not apply to overnight climbing parties holding a wilderness permit. Camping is prohibited at the Cascade Pass trailhead and at Cascade Pass itself.
access.closures: Cascade River Road is prone to storm-damage washout closures — a major washout near milepost 20 closed the road for several weeks in August 2025. Check the NPS Cascade River Road conditions page before driving.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None — this is NPS land, so no Northwest Forest Pass or Discover Pass is required for the trailhead.

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
overnight_permit.where: Camps south of Cache Col are outside the national park. Register at the trailhead if a register is posted.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft. This stretch is well graded, well marked and by far the busiest — it is a popular day hike in its own right.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' path to climber's right, bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over snow or heather across the east flanks of Mixup Peak, crossing a spur ridge, to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. The path is intermittent and in early season it is under snow, when route-finding matters more and the traverse has a bad runout.

Ascend moderate snow — up to about 35 degrees — to Cache Col at roughly 6,900-6,960 ft. The glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but carry an axe and often crampons depending on firmness. Late season Cache Col itself can moat out and become awkward to cross.

From Cache Col make a descending traverse south-southeast, losing about 600 ft, to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for Magic Mountain and for the Ptarmigan Traverse, with reliable water. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip rather than a car-to-car push.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking; overnight camping at Kool-Aid Lake needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount for the Cascade River Road areas.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Snow-covered traverse below Mixup with a poor runout in early season
Cache Col moats out and becomes awkward late season
Loose rock on the summit tower ledges
The false summit — parties stop there or commit to the wrong side of it
No water on the upper ridge; last reliable source is Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Ridge starts at the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, at about 7,100 ft. From Kool-Aid Lake it is roughly 1,000 ft of straightforward heather and scree straight up to that col — there is no gully to pick and no notch to confuse, which makes this the most forgiving base on this list to arrive at.

The route-finding problem is not the base but the top, and it is worth knowing before you set off. The first third of the ridge is an easy heather scramble, with possible snow, leading to a false summit about 300 ft southeast of the true summit. That false summit is the landmark that tells you you are on route, and it is also where parties stop, believing they have topped out.

From the false summit the way on is counter-intuitive: find a dirty gully on the right and downclimb about 80 ft, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew around the east and northeast side of the summit tower. A hand line or a belay is worth having, and the descent goes back down the climbing route.

In poor visibility the two things to hold onto are that the col is the low point on the skyline between Magic and Hurry-Up, and that if you are standing on a high point with more rock still above you across a gap, you are on the false summit and need to lose height on the right before regaining it.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for roughly the first half, then gravel and rougher for the remaining miles to the Cascade Pass trailhead; regularly damaged by flooding of the Cascade River
road.driveNote: 23.1 miles from SR-20 at Marblemount to the trailhead, about a 1-hour drive. Subject to sudden washout closures (e.g., a multi-week closure near MP 20 in August 2025) — check current NPS road-conditions postings before you go.
road.seasonalGate: Gated/closed to vehicles each winter at Eldorado Creek (milepost 20), about 3 miles before the trailhead; reopening date varies year to year with snowpack and storm damage

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass ($5/day equivalent) for trailhead parking; the wilderness permit itself is free to obtain in person at Marblemount, though Recreation.gov charges a small fee for advance-reserved permits
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the Mount Shuksan, Eldorado Peak and Forbidden Peak cross-country zones, which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry wilderness permit required for camping, issued by the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount for the Inspiration zone
access.closures: Cascade River Road is gated and closed to vehicles in winter; check NPS road-conditions page for current washout/closure status
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS) / Stephen Mather Wilderness
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass at the Eldorado Creek Trailhead

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount; $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee.

approach_variants.name: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
approach_variants.notes: Everything below the ice cap is the standard Eldorado approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, backtrack a short way along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River (a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts year to year), then the steep unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,000-3,500 ft through old growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine meadows of Eldorado Creek basin — commonly five to six hours from the car. Push on to the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,600 ft. From that camp it is roughly a 45-minute roped glacier walk north-northwest to where the towers rise out of the icecap. The towers sit at the saddle you cross anyway to get from the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister — so most parties pass beneath them on the way to Klawatti, Austera or Dorado Needle and climb one as a side objective. Round trip from camp is well under two hours.
approach_variants.season: Once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower has opened enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late in the season — usually July or August, most often as part of an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach — roped travel and crevasse rescue gear, not an unroped stroll
The moat where the glacier rests against the rock, which is the whole gate on this climb
Loose rock near the summit
Softening snow bridges on the return, which is the real time constraint on such a short objective
approach_variants.baseFinding: Tepeh Towers is an arête of many spires, not one tower — that is the first thing to understand, and it is why the base finding here has to be about the moat rather than about the skyline. The formation is a rock arête poking out of the icecap northwest of the Inspiration Glacier, with Eldorado to the west and Klawatti to the northeast, and it carries a great many small spires. So the procedure is: climb high on the glacier until the ice is resting against the rock, and cross the moat there. You are looking for the point where the snow meets the rock cleanly enough to step across; that point, not a particular spire seen from a distance, is what you navigate to. The positive confirmation is fixed gear, and it is the only discriminator published for this formation: the Tower Parties climb has rappel anchors directly below its summit. If you top out and there is no anchor below you, you have climbed a neighbouring spire — which is not dangerous here, but it is not the recorded line either. The length test is short and unambiguous: one short low-fifth pitch above the moat, then scrambling to the top. If you are running out a second and third rope length, you are on something else on the same arête. What is honestly not known: no published account names which of the spires is the climbed one or gives a way to tell it from its neighbours at a distance. That gap is stated here rather than filled — treat the anchor below the summit as the confirmation and the moat as the navigation.

road.name: Cascade River Road (from Marblemount) to Boston Basin/Eldorado trailhead area
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel with potholes and washboard; passenger cars can often reach mile ~18 (NP boundary) but a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for the final miles to the Eldorado TH/Boston Basin pulloff (~mile 20-21.7). Vulnerable to washouts/flooding closures, especially in spring and after heavy rain.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3-3.5 hours from Seattle to Marblemount, then 45 min-1+ hour further up Cascade River Road to the trailhead area.
road.seasonalGate: Only snow-cleared and opened each spring/early summer; check the NPS North Cascades road-conditions page before driving.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH
waypoints.directions: From Seattle, take I-5 north then follow WA-20, the North Cascades Highway, east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit; reserve in advance on Recreation.gov or pick up a limited walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp
waypoints.directions: Walk back a short way along the road to the current crossing of the Cascade River, a log or a braided ford that shifts year to year, then climb the steep unmaintained climbers' path through old growth to a boulder field, cross Eldorado Creek and continue into the Eldorado Creek basin meadows. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier to the camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet.

waypoints.name: Base of Tepeh Towers
waypoints.note: ~45 min glacier walk N/NW from camp to where the towers rise off the Eldorado ice cap.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and walk the glacier north-northwest for about 45 minutes to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arete that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: Tepeh Towers
waypoints.note: One short low-5th-class pitch above the moat, then a scramble to the top.
waypoints.directions: Climb high on the glacier to where it rests against the rock and cross the moat. One short low-fifth-class pitch, then easy scrambling, leads to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.

access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
