approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm bench and the Cache Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft. Follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to the pass at roughly 5,400 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill at a creek crossing lower down.

At the pass, near the benches, turn right (south) onto the obvious climbers' path — do not continue on the maintained trail toward Stehekin. The path bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across heather and talus on the flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge.

This traverse crosses steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. In early season the runout is bad — a slip has a drop of several hundred feet below it — so an ice axe and genuine comfort on firm snow traverses are the entry requirement, not optional extras.

Continue to the toe of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000-6,200 ft. The described landmark is a seasonal waterfall: walk past it, turn right, and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so this is either a long car-to-car day of 7-9 hours to the summit, or you continue past the notch to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft) or near Cache Col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; access gets harder through August as the Cache Glacier recedes
hazards: Steep snow gullies on the traverse with a bad runout in early season
Wrong notch — U-notch on the left versus V-notch on the right
Bergschrunds flanking the snow tongue, ten to fifteen feet down to rock
Rockfall, natural and climber-triggered, on the upper gullies and staircase
Moat at the glacier-rock junction, worsening through the season and year on year
No camping permitted at Cascade Pass or on Mixup Arm
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two notches at the head of the Cache Glacier on Mixup's east side, and picking the wrong one is the standard mistake.

A U-shaped notch sits on the left and a V-shaped notch on the right. The East Face is accessed from the V-notch. It is common — and accepted — to go up through the U-notch on the left and wrap around the back side to reach the V, so being at the U is not a failure, but starting to climb from it is.

Gunsight Notch, the prominent notch west of Cache Col, is the portal that serves Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, and the snow tongue leading to it is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees. Bergschrunds flank the tongue on either side, dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and the ground between the snow and the rock is wet, tight and swept by rockfall.

From the south side of the notch the sequence is specific and is your confirmation: go west about 100 ft down a side gully, then ascend northwest up a wide, loose gully to a saddle. At that saddle the White Staircase begins — an easy, exposed class 3 staircase of pale grey rock on the right-hand side of the large summit pyramid. If you are looking at a grey staircase-like ramp on the right side of the pyramid, you are exactly where you should be.

The hardest and dirtiest climbing on the whole approach is the first fifty feet out of the moat where the glacier meets rock — perhaps mid-fifth on loose ground. That difficulty is itself a tell: if the entry felt trivial, check that you have actually crossed the moat at the right place.

Season matters for this specifically. As the Cache Glacier recedes, getting to the notch has been getting harder year on year, and by August the moat can be the deciding problem rather than the climbing.

road.name: Cascade River Road (leaves SR 20 at Marblemount)
road.status: Paved for ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel to the Cascade Pass trailhead at about MP 23.1. NPS listed the road as open on its road-conditions page as of 3 July 2026 and no longer lists the June 2026 vehicle closure at Eldorado Creek (MP 20), which while in force left about three miles each way to the trailhead on foot or bike. Washouts and landslides have closed this road at Eldorado Creek repeatedly over the years, so check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
road.driveNote: 23.1 miles of paved-then-gravel road from SR 20 at Marblemount to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (NPS-confirmed distance). The road has washed out repeatedly in recent years — check the park's road-conditions page immediately before a trip.
road.seasonalGate: Even in normal years the road is typically gated in winter/early spring and doesn't fully reopen to the Cascade Pass Trailhead until snowmelt clears it, usually late May-June.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23.1 mi from Marblemount; Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road (FR 15) to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at about 3,600 ft, 23.1 miles from Marblemount. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, with a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; North Cascades backcountry permits should be reserved at least two days ahead if you plan to camp.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction with post marked for Stehekin; leave the maintained trail here and head south up open heather/talus toward the Ptarmigan Traverse.
waypoints.directions: Follow the well-graded, switchbacking Cascade Pass Trail 3.5 to 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill up at a creek crossing lower on the trail.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Traverse the lower Cache Glacier below Cache Col; rope up for crevasses, softening snow bridges by midday in summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pass do not continue on the maintained Stehekin trail. Pick up the climbers' path on the right, south side that bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across the heather and talus of Mixup Arm and Mix-up's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge and several steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. Early in the season those gullies have poor runout above a drop of some 400 ft, so an ice axe and comfort traversing firm snow matter here. The traverse ends at the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 to 6,200 ft, where crevasses warrant a rope in early to mid season.

waypoints.name: Gunsight Notch
waypoints.note: Narrow gap in the ridge (portal used for Mix-up, Triplets and Cascade Peak); pass through and drop into the basin below Mix-up's east face - also the rappel exit on descent.
waypoints.directions: Ascend moderate glaciated and snow slopes toward the obvious notch system below and left of the summit, the so-called V-notch just north of Gunsight Notch, the main portal between Mix-up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak. Gain the notch by a short snow or scree gully; the technical crux for many parties is exiting the bergschrund or moat below it, which can reach mid-5th class on loose, dirty rock. Note that camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so parties either do this as a long day or camp on past toward Kool-Aid Lake or Cache Col.

waypoints.name: East Face rock bands / gullies
waypoints.note: Ledge-and-gully system through broken rock bands leading to the summit block; loose rock common, watch for parties above.
waypoints.directions: From the south side of the notch work up Class 3-4 ramps on the east side to the light-gray feature climbers call the White Staircase, exposed but generally solid Class 3 with loose, dirty sections. It leads to a shoulder below the summit pyramid and on to a point roughly 100 ft below the top where the roped pitches begin. Rockfall, both natural and climber-triggered, is a real hazard through these gullies, so keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.

waypoints.name: Mix-up Peak Summit
waypoints.note: Low fifth-class summit moves gain the true summit; descend via several rappels back through Gunsight Notch.
waypoints.directions: The last hundred feet or so steepens into a short, sustained low- to mid-5th-class step on compact, occasionally dirty rock, protected with natural gear rather than bolts. It tops out on the exposed summit ridge a few yards from the true summit, leaving a short unroped scramble to the top before the rappel descent begins.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: North Cascades Backcountry Permit
access.closures: Campfires banned in all portions of the North Cascades NPS Complex since 29 June 2026; Washington statewide burn ban from 2 August 2026
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.land_manager: National Park Service

overnight_permit.what: No permit for camps south of Cache Col; North Cascades NP wilderness permit for any camp on the Cascade Pass side
overnight_permit.where: Park permits come from Recreation.gov or the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. South of Cache Col is Glacier Peak Wilderness, where no permit is needed.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the Ptarmigan Traverse to the Spider-Formidable col
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft at the end of the Cascade River Road. The maintained trail runs 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft — well graded, an hour and a half to two hours at a steady pace. Everything beyond is bootpath and it is the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse.

From the pass take the bootpath uphill to the south and traverse along Mix-Up Arm on heather, talus and snow, then up the mellow Cache Glacier to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft — corniced early in the season. From the col, a descending traverse south-south-east on more heather, talus and snow reaches Kool-Aid Lake at 6,100 ft, the standard base camp, roughly three hours and five to six miles from Cascade Pass.

South past Art's Knoll comes the Red Ledge: an exposed traverse over loose rock and lingering snow patches that many parties rope for, and by common consent the crux of the approach. It is noticeably worse when snow-covered.

Beyond it a rough path runs about a mile over meadow, snow, talus and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall at around 6,500 ft. Rope up, ascend the glacier's left side weaving through crevasses, and reach the Spider-Formidable col at 7,320 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, best late Jul-Aug
hazards: the Red Ledge — loose rock, exposed, and materially worse when snow-covered
cornice at Cache Col early in the season
crevasses on the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall
steep snow and moat immediately below the Spider-Formidable notch
loose rock in the gullies on the south face
long, remote position with no maintained trail beyond Cascade Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the part that is easy to get wrong, and it is a counting exercise rather than a description.

From the col, go through the narrow eastern notch and descend roughly 150 vertical feet of steep snow — or in the moat beside it — before it becomes feasible to start contouring right, to the west. Do not try to contour immediately from the notch; you have to lose that height first.

Continue west over slabs and snow, then heather and small rock outcrops. Leave the snow onto class 3 rock, climb up and then left to a distinct ledge. From that ledge make a rising traverse to the north-west, scrambling across two gullies. Then cross a spur ridge to reach a third gully — and it is the third gully that you climb.

So the test is: from the ledge, the first two gullies are crossed, not entered. If you start up the first gully you meet after the ledge you will be on steeper, looser ground short of the line. If you have crossed a spur ridge and are looking up a gully, that is the one.

Some trip reports also describe reaching the south-face snow alcove from a staging camp near a notch at about 7,050 ft below the col, by either a hidden gully on the left with fifth-class moves or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right at class 3 with one harder step. The right-hand ledge is the usual choice; if you are pulling fifth-class moves you have taken the left option.

road.name: Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15)
road.status: Paved to about mile 10, then gravel with potholes and washboard to its end at mile 22.3 (Cascade Pass Trailhead, 3,600 ft). The June 2026 vehicle closure at milepost 20 (Eldorado) for storm/flood repairs has been lifted; the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open.
road.driveNote: No RVs, large trailers, or vehicles over 22 feet on the upper, narrower gravel section.
road.seasonalGate: Cascade River Road (FR-15) and the Cascade Pass trailhead typically open by early-mid summer, depending on snowpack.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR 15); day-use register at the kiosk, overnight climbers need a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the very end of Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15), at about 3,600 feet. Day users sign in at the register on the kiosk there. Climbers staying out overnight need a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center before starting up the trail.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends at this saddle; climbers leave the trail here and traverse cross-country up Mixup Arm toward the Cache Glacier.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Rocky notch atop the Cache Glacier on the Skagit/Chelan county line; crampons/axe recommended for the glacier crossing just below it early season.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small, heavily-used tarn camp in the cirque below Cache Col at the head of the Middle Fork Cascade River; running water nearby.

waypoints.name: Spider-Formidable Col
waypoints.note: Reached via a traverse of the Middle Cascade Glacier to this notch between Spider Mountain and Formidable; watch for crevasses on the glacier approach.

waypoints.name: Yang Yang Lakes
waypoints.note: Alternate camp in the Flat Creek cirque reached by dropping south off the col; base for the traverse onto Formidable's south face.

waypoints.name: Red Ledges (below Art's Knoll)
waypoints.note: Broad Class 3 sandstone ledge system that's benign when dry but has serious exposure and route-finding trouble if snow-covered.

waypoints.name: Mount Formidable
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a sandstone ramp and a short, exposed Class 4-5 cleft just below the top; loose rock has been the scene of at least one fatality here.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: Backcountry permit required ($10 + $6 fee) from North Cascades Visitor Center in Marblemount. Best climbing season: late July through September. Located within North Cascades National Park. Large paved parking available at trailhead.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry/climbing permit required for any overnight stay; $10 per person camping fee plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee, booked via Recreation.gov and activated in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount before setting out.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter, typically early December to mid/late April, at gates near Ross Dam (MP134) and Silver Star (MP171); in 2026 spring damage and emergency repairs pushed the full reopening to June 14 — check WSDOT's SR-20 pass report before an early- or late-season trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No park entrance fee, but some SR-20 trailhead parking areas require a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit, fee per person
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or pick up a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

approach_variants.name: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead off SR-20 near Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound about ten miles, losing steadily along Bridge Creek, to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp. Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail and head upstream; it gets brushier and less maintained the further you go, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek.

Around mile 13-14 the maintained tread effectively ends. Ford the North Fork — cold and sometimes knee deep, and easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn — then work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall draining toward the Goode Glacier, which is the way to avoid the worst brush. Look for the alder tunnel: a boot-path corridor through the slide alder that saves a great deal of thrashing.

Camp around the glacier toe at roughly 5,400-6,800 ft depending on how far you push. Plan on three to four days round trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late July through September. The moat crossing is easiest once the glacier has receded, around the third week of July, and gets harder again as the season goes on
hazards: A moat and bergschrund at the toe of the buttress with a steep step of about 50 degrees where the route steps off the Goode Glacier onto rock — worse as the season goes on, and reported by some parties as impassable late
Open crevasses and overhead serac hazard on the Goode Glacier
Loose and wet rock on the approach slabs beside the waterfall
Cornices on the approach in early season
A route that is difficult to retreat from once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window
A descent by the Southwest Couloir that several parties report taking 8-10 hours from summit to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark is a colour: the red ledges at the toe of the buttress. Three independent accounts name them, and one quotes a published description doing so. You are looking for a band of red rock where the Goode Glacier meets the foot of the buttress. If the rock in front of you is grey, keep looking along the toe.

The base is the moat at those ledges, and how you cross it is the measure of the season: a collapsed or intact snow bridge, a jump, a downclimb, or a short rappel followed by re-climbing on the far side. Published elevations for this point range from about 6,400 to 7,800 ft across different years and different parties, which is a real disagreement rather than a single number — the glacier has retreated and the crossing point moves. Navigate to the red ledges, not to an altitude.

Above the moat, expect one or two pitches of low fifth on precarious blocks, trending climber's right to gain the buttress crest proper. If your first ground above the glacier is clean and solid, you are not on the toe.

Tell it from the peak's other long route by whether you ever touched the glacier: Megalodon Ridge is gained from the east without crossing the Goode Glacier at all. If you crossed a moat off glacier ice, you are on the Northeast Buttress. If you never left brush and rock, you are on Megalodon.

Confirm as you climb: over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class on the crest, often soloed or simul-climbed, then around 8,000 ft a short unprotectable 5.7 slab on the crest that most parties deviate right to avoid, then roughly five pitches of 5.4-5.5 easing toward the summit. A route that is hard from the bottom is not this one.

road.name: SR 20 / Bridge Creek trailhead
road.status: Paved highway to trailhead
road.driveNote: Highway typically reopens late spring
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 closed in winter

waypoints.name: Bridge Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the Bridge Creek Trailhead at about milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass; the lot is on the north side of the highway, and a short connector trail across the road joins the Pacific Crest Trail southbound. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, and overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: PCT / North Fork Junction
waypoints.directions: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound, losing height steadily along Bridge Creek, for about 10 miles to the junction with the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail near North Fork Camp.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and head upstream; it grows brushier and less maintained, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek. Where the tread fades around mile 13 to 14, ford the North Fork a few steps upstream at a cairn, climb scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the big waterfall draining the Goode Glacier, and follow the alder tunnel through the slide alder to camp near the glacier toe.

waypoints.name: Goode Summit
waypoints.directions: Cross the Goode Glacier, watching for crevasses and serac fall, to the band of red ledges at the toe of the buttress, and get across the moat there. One or two low fifth-class pitches on loose blocks trend right to the crest; follow over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class, step right around a short unprotectable 5.7 slab near 8,000 ft, then climb about five pitches of 5.4 to 5.5 easing to the summit.

waypoints.name: Black Tooth Notch (Rappels)
waypoints.directions: From the summit, make three rappels down along the ridge to Black Tooth Notch. The first runs nearly straight down the ridgeline; the second and third traverse to rappeller's left, so watch the rope tails for snags. Anchors are slung horns and blocks, and a single 60 m rope reaches every station.

waypoints.name: SW Couloir Exit
waypoints.directions: From the notch, cross the exposed 4th-class ledge, then make about three more single-rope rappels into the Southwest Couloir and downclimb class 3 below them. Where the gully narrows into cliffs lower down, exit left onto easier ground rather than rappelling the waterfall band.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Drive SR-20 to milepost 159, a little over a mile east of Rainy Pass, and park in the lot on the north side of the highway.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable permit fee, charged mid-May through early October; no charge the rest of the year; free for youth 15 and under.
access.notes: No trailhead or parking fee - the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek begins on National Park Service land, where no Northwest Forest Pass is required. No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: NPS wilderness/backcountry permit required for all overnight stays. Reserve in advance on recreation.gov (roughly 15% odds in the 2025 early-access lottery) or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites are walk-up only) up to 24 hours ahead at the Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA (SR 20 milepost 105.3).
access.closures: Thunder Creek Fire: North Cascades National Park's fire-closure list (updated September 14, 2026; no end date given) closes the Thunder Creek Trail from the Fisher Creek Trail junction to Park Creek Pass for the Thunder Creek Fire, along with Junction Camp, Skagit Queen Camp and Thunder Basin Camp (hiker and stock sites), and prohibits cross-country travel from the closed trail. This approach cannot be used past the Fisher Creek junction while it stands. The southern approach from Stehekin is closed too: the same list closes the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge, and the High Bridge area, for the Sisi Fire. The Colonial Creek trailhead itself is west of SR 20's winter closure gates (MP 134-171) and is reachable by car year-round. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (NPS) — Ross Lake National Recreation Area / North Cascades National Park
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota reservation or walk-up
overnight_permit.where: Reserve a night-by-night itinerary online via Recreation.gov during the early-access lottery, or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites) at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount up to 24 hours ahead.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
camps: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in
approach_variants.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
approach_variants.season: July and August
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season as the snow finger melts, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft can hold snow or ice
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Hazardous footlog crossings over Thunder Creek at night or high water; no fixed anchors for rappels
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the northeast; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

approach_variants.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead. The way in starts at the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, follows the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then takes the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp, with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.
hazards: Footlog crossing on Park Creek, hazardous at night or in high water
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft above Park Creek Pass can hold snow or ice
Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp; no fixed anchors for rappels
approach_variants.whyThisWay: To cut the Thunder Creek mileage when the boat and shuttle schedule suits you; fewer miles, but the Lake Chelan ferry, the Stehekin bus and a footlog crossing come with it.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20) to Colonial Creek Campground
road.status: Open year-round to this trailhead
road.driveNote: Colonial Creek Campground/Thunder Creek Trailhead sits at roughly SR 20 milepost 130, on the west (Skagit County) side of the highway.
road.seasonalGate: Not applicable — trailhead is outside the MP134-171 winter closure zone

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead (Colonial Creek Campground)
waypoints.note: Overnight stays need a North Cascades backcountry permit, reserved on Recreation.gov or picked up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount; the trail starts at the south end of Colonial Creek Campground near the boat ramp off SR 20.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to Colonial Creek Campground near milepost 130 on Diablo Lake. The Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground, near the boat ramp, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Junction Camp
waypoints.note: Established hiker/stock camp about 10 miles in; cross a log bridge to the creekside hiker camp with views of Boston Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south along Thunder Arm and up the Thunder Creek valley, past McAllister and Tricouni camps, about 10 miles to Junction Camp at the Fisher Creek Trail junction. The last mile or so below the camp is a steep climb.

waypoints.name: Park Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Broad, flat, rocky trough at Thunder Creek's headwaters; leave the maintained trail here and head east into the moraine toward the Fremont Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Thunder Creek Trail rather than turning onto the Fisher Creek Trail, and continue up the upper Thunder Creek valley past Thunder Basin to Park Creek Pass, a broad, rocky trough at about 6,000 ft at the head of the creek.

waypoints.name: Point 8248 / Fremont Glacier saddle camp
waypoints.note: Rock-outcrop bivy sites at the southern margin of the Fremont Glacier with nearby running water; standard high camp for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and climb east about 500 ft into the moraine, then traverse north around a broad ridge over heather and rock for roughly 1.5 to 2 miles, crossing a rib near 7,600 ft and a gully through cliff bands that can hold snow or ice, to the bivy sites on the saddle at the southern edge of the Fremont Glacier.

waypoints.name: Fremont Glacier hogsback and bergschrund
waypoints.note: Rope up for glacier travel; the snow hogback at the upper edge of the glacier can leave a bergschrund exposed in late season.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and make the gentle glacier crossing north from camp to the Hogsback, the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier. Late in the season a bergschrund and a moat can open where the snow meets the rock.

waypoints.name: Western ramp / U-notch summit ridge gain
waypoints.note: A Class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp (a fault-line weakness) to the summit ridge, then exposed Class 2-3 ledges lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and south horn.
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat onto rock and climb a Class 3-4 pitch to a left-slanting ramp, a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands, which leads up to the summit ridge. Do not head straight at the summit tower from the glacier.

waypoints.name: Mount Logan Summit
waypoints.note: Tiny summit gained via a final Class 3-4 rock pitch; reverse via the same route with a short rappel off the summit block.
waypoints.directions: Traverse exposed Class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge through the U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn, then climb a final Class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on solid rock to the tiny summit.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
approach_variants.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
hazards: Gated trailhead tied to SR-20 seasonal closure limits when this way in is open
Crossing of a 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin before dropping to the lake camp
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow; snow bridge collapse risk on the Banded Glacier
Crevasses on the Banded Glacier; talus over hard glacier ice is treacherous in a whiteout
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy summit ridge and rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail route-finding; heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
bivy.notes: Reached via the Fisher Creek Trail fork off the Thunder Creek Trail (~9 miles in); the standard overnight camp below the Banded Glacier.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, the Douglas Creek alder, then the west-side gully to the polished slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 151, about 3,700 ft. Hike 3.5 miles and 2,800 ft to Easy Pass at 6,500 ft, then descend 1.5 miles through alpine meadows and forest into Fisher Basin and down to the Fisher Creek valley floor and the established campsites.

Cross Fisher Creek on a large fallen log and travel the east side of the Douglas Creek valley on a faint climbers' path. This is where the route is actually decided. The transition from forest to open terrain runs into a vast field of slide alder and brush over ten feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, cut by small rocky stream channels — progress measured in inches per minute. One 2022 party was turned back at 4,200 ft by this alone, having covered half a mile an hour for seven hours. The glacier travel is superb and the bushwhack miserable.

Above the brush, the way onto the glacier is a gully on the west side of the basin. Then it is glacier travel to the col and a short summit block.
approach_variants.season: June and July for the best glacier conditions
hazards: A slide-alder thicket over ten feet high that has defeated at least one party outright, with heavy mosquito and black-fly pressure
Cliff bands ringing the Fisher Basin cirque
Crevasses and glide cracks reported over 20 ft deep on the Douglas Glacier
A steep, exposed rock ramp of roughly 300 ft above camp that is hard to protect
Steep icy summit snow needing solid crampon and axe technique
Steep loose-rock switchbacks on the Easy Pass trail itself above mile 2.5
approach_variants.baseFinding: The gully is on the west side of the basin and it is identified by what it delivers you onto, not by its entrance. It starts class 3, steepens quickly to class 4 or low fifth for a short section that is hard to protect, and tops out on glacier-polished slabs. Polished slabs above a short steep step is the confirmation. From there it is about 1,500 vertical ft of scrambling on those slabs to the toe of the Douglas Glacier. So the order is: brush, gully, polished slabs, glacier. If you are on slabs without having climbed a short hard step, you have not been through the gully. The route joins its neighbour near the top and that is expected: ascend the Douglas Glacier — steep at its head — to the col, then traverse to meet the Banded Glacier and finish up the same class 3-4 summit block, about 300 vertical ft. A summit block reached without crossing to a second glacier means you are still on the Douglas side of the col. The approach is the strongest discriminator on this mountain, because all three routes end at the same summit but none of them share a valley. This route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek drainage on the northeast. The Banded Glacier comes from Fisher Creek to a lake camp at 5,160 ft and crosses a col onto the Banded. The Fremont Glacier comes from Thunder Creek and Park Creek Pass on the southeast. If you passed Park Creek Pass this morning, you are not on the Douglas. And the honest gap: no source publishes a countable marker for the gully entrance itself — it is described only as being on the west side of the basin. The polished slabs above it are the reliable confirmation, which means you find out you were right after the hard part.

waypoints.directions: Hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.5 miles to Easy Pass, descend into Fisher Basin to the Fisher Creek valley floor, cross the creek on a large fallen log, and follow a faint path up the east side of the Douglas Creek valley through dense slide alder. approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
camps: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir; a fatal accident on record
Loose Class 3-4 rock in the gully, with parties above and below
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse and buried creek channels
Couloir can be melted out to rock in late season
Short glacier crossing on the Taboo Glacier, firm snow or ice early season
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

approach_variants.name: Torment Basin climbers' path

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely contested — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade River Road at the river bridge, about a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead

approach_variants.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
approach_variants.season: midsummer once brush is passable
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach, so less current information on conditions
Loose crumbly rock on the climb and rockfall onto parties below
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
Biting insects on the approach
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Late season, when the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier makes the standard line hard; steeper and brushier on the approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

Park at the small roadside pullout. Register and pick up your permit through Marblemount before heading up.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin
waypoints.directions: Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then turn sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. It switchbacks up through forest across four small creeks to treeline and the low camps around 5,300 ft, then continues up open slabs and tundra on the skier's right of Boston Creek to high camp near 6,200 to 6,400 ft.

waypoints.name: Base of south ridge
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail and make a rising traverse northwest near the 6,200 ft contour beneath Forbidden Peak's south spur, crossing a prominent rock rib below the cliffs. Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's left and follow it up to the deep couloir breaking the rock band on the left; cross the bergschrund or moat and scramble about 100 ft of loose class 3-4 to the notch.

waypoints.name: Mount Torment summit
waypoints.directions: Climb an open book angling left off the notch, turn right at its top to a ledge, and take a short second open book to the crest. Pass a steeper tower on sloping, exposed ledges, weave among towers continuing leftward on the southwest face, and finish on sustained fourth and low fifth-class granite to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp and the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The traverse starts by climbing Torment's South Ridge, so the approach is the South Ridge approach. From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount), take the old mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four creek crossings, treeline at about 5,300 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft — call it 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft from the car.

From high camp traverse the upper basin northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, beneath Forbidden's south spur, crossing a rock rib and a couple of snowmelt channels, heading for the toe of the Taboo Glacier and the lower South Ridge.

Because the traverse is long and committing, many parties instead carry over and camp at about 7,100 ft on the Taboo directly under Torment's southeast face at the foot of the east couloir, which turns a very long day into a reasonable one. Others bivy on the ridge partway across.

Overnight permits for Boston Basin are picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Moat and bergschrund at the foot of the east couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 gully with parties above
Whiteout navigation across the basin-to-glacier traverse
Early-season avalanche exposure and buried creek crossings
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The traverse's start is the same notch that starts the South Ridge, and finding it is a glacier problem, not a rock problem.

Rope up at the toe of the Taboo and follow the glacier up on its climber's-left side, watching for crevasses. You are looking for the one deep gully that breaks the rock band on the left — the east couloir. A bergschrund and a moat sit at its base; the moat where the glacier pulls away from rock can require a short awkward move onto rock, and this crossing is where a picket, axe and crampons for the leader earn their weight.

Above the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 to the notch. Standing in the notch you are on the crest with Torment Basin dropping away to the west and the Taboo below to the east — that two-sided view is the confirmation that you are at the base of the climbing and not partway up a blind break in the rock band.

Later in the season, when the moat is bad, parties cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain it from the Torment Basin side instead. Adjacent scrambling lines that avoid the snow couloir and rejoin the same notch are also described.

The whole basin-to-glacier traverse is genuinely easy to lose in a whiteout — it is uniform open ground with no trail — so if you cannot see the Taboo, do not start the traverse on dead reckoning alone.

waypoints.name: Mount Torment summit
waypoints.note: Leave packs at the notch just below the top, tag the summit, and downclimb back to the notch.
waypoints.directions: Traverse northwest across the upper basin to the toe of the Taboo Glacier, rope up, and climb it and the east couloir past the moat to the notch at the base of Torment's South Ridge. Climb the ridge to Torment's summit.

waypoints.name: Forbidden Peak summit
waypoints.directions: From the notch below Torment's summit, rappel onto the Forbidden Glacier, cross it to the saddle, and follow the Sidewalk in the Sky crest to the West Ridge Notch and up Forbidden's West Ridge to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Round to the unnamed glacier north of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
This is a genuinely obscure line and every recorded approach to it is a variation on getting round to the mountain's north side, which no other Primus route visits.

The first recorded ascent reached it from the Klawatti side: descend a couloir where the North Klawatti Glacier meets Primus's west ridge, then traverse an unnamed glacier north of Primus to the foot of the crest. The first-ascent account says in as many words that it was unlikely this approach had been used before.

Other parties have come from the Thunder Creek side instead — the same trailhead, creek crossing at McAllister Camp and climbers' trail up the ridge as the East Slope, to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the toe of the Borealis Glacier — and then reached the ridge by circling the glacial lake at the glacier's terminus and crossing a short section of glacier to the base, rather than climbing the glacier toward Lucky Pass. One party took that line specifically because conditions at the standard Primus-Tricouni saddle were hazardous that day.

The ridge itself is about 1,000 ft and took the first-ascent party roughly an hour.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August; a documented late-September attempt found the crux notch glazed with bullet ice and the loose rock unbonded, which made the route markedly harder and more dangerous
hazards: Very loose, serrated rock along the entire crest — blocks and towers described as good but somewhat loose
A 5.6 crux notch with no fixed protection: natural gear and slung blocks only
Verglas glazing the notch in cool or wet weather, which is what defeated a late-September attempt
Committing retreat once above the crux — the recommended descent is the East Ridge to Lucky Pass, not this ridge
Glacier travel on an unnamed, rarely visited glacier with no established line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is which side of the mountain you are on, and it is decided by whether you had to go down to get there. Every approach to this ridge involves losing height onto a glacier north of Primus — down a couloir from the North Klawatti Glacier where it meets Primus's west ridge, or down and around the glacial lake at the Borealis Glacier's terminus. If your day has been a continuous climb, you have not reached this route.

The negative test is unambiguous and it is the one to carry: Lucky Pass is not this route. If you are standing at a col at about 7,200 ft at the head of the Borealis Glacier, with Tricouni Peak's route splitting off east, you are at the start of the East Slope — a class 3 walk. The North Ridge is reached by turning away from that pass, not through it.

What the base itself looks like: the foot of a 1,000 ft crest of blocks and towers, met from a glacier rather than from a notch. There is no published cairn, marker or fixed anchor at the start; the ridge is very rarely repeated and nothing on it should be assumed to be in place.

Confirm on the ground you climb, not on the approach: the lower ridge is 3rd and 4th class blocks and towers; the upper ridge is banded rock at low fifth, and that banding is what the first-ascent party singled out. A ridge that stays third class to the summit is not this one — and a ridge that never carried you above a glacier on the peak's north side never was.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
approach_variants.hours: Half a day from Boston Basin camp
approach_variants.notes:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; July and August are the most settled, and snow can linger around camp into July
hazards: Rockfall off the ridge and the tower is the primary hazard
Weather that builds fast, with afternoon thunderstorms usual
A very small, exposed tower top that many parties choose not to stand on
Approach terrain shared with Forbidden's West Ridge descent, so parties may be above you in the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The formation is the easy part: the aiguille is conspicuous on entering Boston Basin and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

The base is the notch to the right of the north ridge — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

Count the pitches, because the count is the route: three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling to the base of a tower, and then one 40-ft pitch to its top. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

The most important thing to know about the top is that it is not the top. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

Tell it from the south ridge by which side you walked round. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.

Three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling reach the base of a tower; a 40-ft 5.5 pitch gains its top. The route ends here: the true high point beyond looks ready to topple and most parties do not go to it.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, the traverse corridor to the Red Ledge, and the Formidable Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A deep objective reached along the same corridor as its neighbours, and the walk-in is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain rather than a hike. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, take the maintained trail to the pass, then leave it and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow bands, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake, climb out of the basin toward the cliff band running west off the knoll above; the Red Ledge cuts through it, usually entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and a few feet of easy rock, and it is broad and walkable unless it is holding snow or verglas. Roughly a quarter mile past the ledge, descend several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between the two large icefall sections, cross that bench, and continue to the foot of the Formidable Glacier. Note that this is a different objective from the peak's ordinary walk-up on the south side, which is the descent line rather than the approach.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer suits it best: early enough that the couloir still holds firm snow or ice rather than bare, rockfall-prone rock, but late enough that the moat at the top of the glacier has opened enough to allow access to the face.
hazards: large blocks have come down on this route
the approach crosses above a heavily crevassed glacier
the standard descent on the south side has difficult route-finding, constant exposure and loose rock, and has been the scene of a fatality
a snow couloir that steepens past sixty-five degrees with overhanging chockstones at its top
sparse protection on the crux, with one long pitch reported as protected by a single piece
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go right on the glacier, and the moat is the gate. Ascend the Formidable Glacier by traversing right, to its northern end, and climbing the easier, safer section there — the direct line up the middle weaves through many large cracks and is not the way. At the top of the glacier, stop and hunt along the margin for a place to cross the large moat, because that crossing, not the climbing, decides whether the route goes at all on a given day. Above the moat, the route begins in a rubble-covered fourth-class gully, and the rubble is the identifier: this is broken, dirty ground rather than clean rock, and it feeds directly into a snow couloir hidden from below. If what rises above your moat crossing is clean, steep rock with no rubble gully and no couloir behind it, you are too far along the face and should traverse back toward the glacier's northern end. Once in the couloir it steepens past sixty-five degrees in a couple of spots, with good cracks for rock protection on its right side and overhanging chockstones to pull through at the top, landing on a large ledge. The crux above that is two pitches around a loose thirty-foot granite tower split by a three-foot crack — if you have not passed a tower like that, the crux is still ahead of you.

road.name: Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15)
road.status: Paved to about mile 10, then gravel with potholes and washboard to its end at mile 22.3 (Cascade Pass Trailhead, 3,600 ft).
road.driveNote: Roughly 3.5-4 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to Marblemount, then the Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass Trailhead at its end, followed by a long wilderness approach. No RVs, large trailers, or vehicles over 22 feet on the upper gravel section.
road.seasonalGate: Closed by snow in winter, historically near Eldorado Creek around milepost 20; the road reopens to the trailhead as snowmelt and repairs allow, typically over late spring and early summer.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount.
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto the Cascade River Road and follow it 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead, about 3,600 ft. The first third is paved and the rest is gravel, narrow and steep near the end; the upper road usually opens by late June or early July.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here and head south toward the Mixup flank.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up its long switchbacks through forest and meadow to the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Often corniced on top; the far side drops on steep snow to Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow, then rope up and climb the Cache Glacier to the col.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Camp here; the northeast face is about three hours away.
waypoints.directions: Descend the steep snow on the far side of the col to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake.

waypoints.name: Mount Formidable Summit
waypoints.note: Via Cascade Pass, the Ptarmigan Traverse, and the Middle/Formidable Glaciers; moderate rock to 5.6 with an AI2+ pitch in a hidden couloir.
waypoints.directions: From Kool-Aid Lake climb out of the basin and cross the Red Ledge, then drop several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier and cross to the Formidable Glacier. Climb it on its northern side, cross the moat into the hidden couloir, and follow the face to the north ridge and summit.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

approach_variants.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the Tepeh Towers saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a small col at the toe of the ridge, at the top of the McALLISTER glacier's 30-degree apron, and the thing directly above it is a line of gendarmes on the crest. Gendarmes on the skyline above a small col at the top of the apron is the confirmation.

Cross the moat at the col, not at the snow gully. There is an alternative snow gully nearby that parties sometimes use to gain the ridge, and it is guarded by a large moat that usually still needs a short rappel to bypass. The route's own start is easy fifth-class rock straight off the small col at the toe. If you are eyeing a snow gully with a big gap at its head, you are looking at the alternative, not the route.

The length test is decisive on this peak because the four routes are wildly different lengths: this one is three pitches, each well under 25 m. If you are running full rope lengths, or if you are still climbing after three, you are on the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from the other side) or the East Ridge (a long day off a different col).

A fixed-gear confirmation, and a warning with it: the crest carries a lot of old fixed slings on rock horns left by earlier parties, and higher up a piton marks a slabby section leading to a V-slot gully. Plenty of tat on horns is a sign you are on the trade line — but it is aging tat, an anchor block has failed here before, and it should be backed up rather than trusted.

And know which side of the needle you are on: this route is reached by climbing the McAllister's apron northwest. The Southwest Buttress lines are reached by continuing to the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass and dropping about 700 vertical ft to a snow gully below it. The East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle. Three different cols; check which one you crossed.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel the rest of the way; the Eldorado Creek trailhead is at about mile 20 and the road continues to the Cascade Pass trailhead. NPS listed the road as open on its road-conditions page as of 3 July 2026 and no longer lists the June 2026 vehicle closure at Eldorado Creek. Washouts and landslides have closed this road at Eldorado Creek repeatedly over the years, so check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
road.driveNote: Not suitable for low-clearance vehicles beyond the pavement; vehicles/trailers over 22 ft or 8 ft wide prohibited beyond mile 18.
road.seasonalGate: Typically snow-gated in winter/spring; usually opens to Cascade Pass trailhead by late June in a normal year.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Standard Eldorado Peak approach start; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 20 miles from Marblemount to the large Eldorado Creek trailhead parking area at road mile 20, around 2,100 ft. From the lot, backtrack a short distance downstream to find a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path heading east and upstream on the far bank. This is the shared Eldorado Peak approach, the same start the other Dorado Needle routes use.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp after the first two talus fields, en route to the higher glacier camps.
waypoints.directions: Follow the climbers' path up the west side of Eldorado Creek through forest and talus, staying right of the large windfall area and not crossing the creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad open basin around 5,500 to 5,800 ft with scattered camps.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf used for all Eldorado-area and Dorado Needle objectives.
waypoints.directions: Continue north over more talus and snow onto the Eldorado Glacier and up to the high camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf near 7,400 to 7,600 ft, about 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft from the car.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north from the Inspiration Glacier through this notch in the Tepeh Towers, about 8,000 ft, onto the McAllister Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier to the notch in the Tepeh Towers.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier below the gendarmes
waypoints.note: Ascend the McAllister Glacier to just below Dorado Needle's line of gendarmes; this is the start of the NW Ridge, the easiest (1940 first-ascent) line at 5.4.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to avoid a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season. Climb the steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, northwest to its top below the line of gendarmes, and look for a safe moat crossing.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: Three pitches of class 5.4 rock past the gendarmes gain the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat and climb a short low-fifth-class pitch to the ridge crest, then short pitches of easy fifth-class rock past the gendarmes to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.
