road.driveNote: From Marblemount (SR 20, mile 106), drive Cascade River Road toward its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead (mile 23.1); the Boston Basin climbers' path leaves the road near mile 22.5.
road.seasonalGate: Gated at Eldorado (mile 20) through winter and during washout/storm repairs; typically opens by late June, sometimes not until early July.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small unmarked pullout at roughly mile 22 of Cascade River Road across from Johannesburg Mountain; room for only 6-8 cars and no facilities.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount to the small unmarked pullout just past mile marker 22, across from Johannesburg Mountain, at roughly 3,200 ft. There is room for only six to eight cars and no facilities, so a full pullout leaves you no good options. From the car the route follows the old mining road about three quarters of a mile to the historic mine site before the steep, eroded Boston Basin climbers' path begins.

waypoints.name: Old miner's cabin site (Boston Basin mine relic)
waypoints.note: Remains of a historic mining cabin mark the trail breaking out of forest onto the open basin slopes; steep, eroded tread up to this point.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old mining road about a mile to the old mine site, then climb the steep, eroded climbers' path through forest, crossing several streams, until it breaks out of the trees near 5,300 ft at the remains of an old mining cabin.

waypoints.name: South Fork Boston Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Last easy, reliable creek crossing just below the lower Boston Basin camps; fill up here before heading into the alpine.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the path onto the open basin slopes to the last and largest creek crossing. If the direct crossing looks hard, follow a path along the edge of the ravine to an easier spot where it drops in to cross; fill water here.

waypoints.name: Lower Boston Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry campsites just above treeline; NPS wilderness permit required and food must be stored per park regulations.
waypoints.directions: Across the creek, the path climbs a short way to the lower camps on a moraine ridge with small trees, just below the bare slabs left by the receding Quien Sabe Glacier.

waypoints.name: Western edge of Quien Sabe Glacier
waypoints.note: Climbers leave the upper basin meadows/moraine here and rope up for glacier travel toward Sharkfin Col.
waypoints.directions: Above the lower camps, climb the bare slabs and moraine toward the upper basin, where the high camps sit near 6,400 ft, to the edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier, and rope up.

waypoints.name: Quien Sabe Glacier crevasses / Sharkfin bergschrund
waypoints.note: Large crevasses open on this glacier by late season and a substantial bergschrund forms beneath the couloir below Sharkfin Tower; probe or find a snow bridge.
waypoints.directions: Climb the Quien Sabe Glacier east toward Sharkfin Tower to the bergschrund at the foot of the gully directly below the tower. Crevasses open wide here by late season.

waypoints.name: Notch between Sharkfin Tower and Boston Peak
waypoints.note: Gap on the southeast side of Sharkfin Tower where Boston's northwest ridge begins. The loose gully above the bergschrund below the tower leads up to it; the only known ascent instead came over Sharkfin Tower and traversed a steep hanging snow slope to the base of the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Cross the bergschrund or its moat and climb the gully, snow early in the season and loose scree and rock later, through the rock band to the notch on the tower's southeast side.

waypoints.name: Boston Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; final ridge is extremely loose, friable rock (5.5 X) with serious exposure, and the FA party simply continued their traverse rather than downclimbing, so a separate descent must be planned.
waypoints.directions: There is no established description of the crest. Expect about 1,000 ft of loose, essentially unprotected rock rated 5.5 X, including two pitches straddling the crest, to the summit.

The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is rough gravel; the road can close at the Eldorado parking area at milepost 20.

road.status: Paved, open seasonally
road.driveNote: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east about 24 miles; turn into Colonial Creek Campground just before the highway crosses the Thunder Arm of Diablo Lake.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east about 24 miles. Just past milepost 130, before the highway crosses the Thunder Arm of Diablo Lake, turn into the south side of Colonial Creek Campground and park in the large lot above the boat ramp, at about 1,200 ft. Walk the length of the campground, following signs to the amphitheater, where the Thunder Creek Trail begins.

waypoints.name: Ruby Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: Hike the Thunder Creek Trail about 2 miles; a third of a mile past the bridge, turn left on the Fourth of July Pass Trail and climb steeply to the pass. Near a tall broken stump with old flagging, take the abandoned way trail off the north side northeast through forest, go straight up through blowdown and a rocky rib to a cairn near 4,950 ft, then follow the path up the south ridge and heather benches to open talus and the summit.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to camp, 3-4 more to the col
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Missing the sharp right turn off the mine roadbed onto the climbers' trail
Bergschrund at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, open both sides late season
Rockfall from the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower during the rising traverse
Exposed rock-and-snow ridge above the col, corniced into early summer
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The rock climbing begins at the Boston-Sahale col, and everything below it is glacier work.

The navigational problem on the way up is the bergschrund, at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides late season. Late in the year the standard solution is to traverse climber's right to end-run the schrund, then cut back up and left above it to the col — a party that pushes straight up the fall line into the schrund is not off route so much as too early in the season for that line.

You know you are at the col because the glacier ends against a defined saddle in the rock ridge and the ground on the far side drops away toward Boston Peak. This is where parties unrope and coil.

From the col the route is a short, exposed ridge of rock and snow: a little rock, then an exposed snow traverse south on crampons and axe, well back from the cornice, to the base of the summit block. The block is then finished as on the Sahale Glacier route, by a short chimney-like exit on its south side to the slung rappel block on top.

In poor visibility the col itself is the reliable target: it is the only low saddle at the top of the glacier, and the ridge beyond it cannot be confused with glacier travel.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for roughly the first 10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel/dirt the rest of the way; the Boston Basin pullout is a small unsigned turnout with space for about 10 cars
road.driveNote: About 21–23 miles from Marblemount on Cascade River Road — look for the small unmarked pullout after the Eldorado Trailhead parking and before the Cascade Pass Trailhead lot
road.seasonalGate: Typically opens by late June and can close again with early snow, flooding, or washouts — check the NPS road-conditions page before driving

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road pullout)
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout at mile ~22 of Cascade River Road opposite Johannesburg Mountain, room for 6-8 cars; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: The Boston Basin start is an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road, about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, sitting opposite Johannesburg Mountain. There is no trailhead sign of any kind, so watch your odometer rather than looking for signage — it is easy to drive straight past. The pullout holds six to eight cars and you need a Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camping in Boston Basin needs a North Cascades wilderness permit picked up in person at Marblemount, and the popular sites fill fast in the early-access lottery for peak summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin low camp
waypoints.note: Designated moraine campsite with composting toilet at treeline; most parties continue higher for a shorter summit day.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing the steep, switchbacking climbers' path above the streams to treeline at about 5,300 ft, where the low camp sits on heather benches and moraine.

waypoints.name: Glacier rope-up point beneath Sharkfin Tower
waypoints.note: Where the boot path meets continuous snow on the Quien Sabe Glacier's lower-angle (north/left) side; rope up for crevasses here.
waypoints.directions: From high camp, stay on climber's left and walk moraine and slabs toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower to the toe of the Quien Sabe Glacier. Rope up where the boot path meets continuous snow, around 6,700 ft.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund crossing
waypoints.note: Narrow snow bridge crosses above and left of the bergschrund late-season; crevasses widen through August-September and the crossing point shifts year to year.
waypoints.directions: Make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower onto the flatter part of the glacier, then pick a line up the steeper section between crevasses; the left-hand and more direct lines merge partway up. Cross near 7,600 ft on a snow bridge above and left of the bergschrund; the crossing point shifts from year to year.

waypoints.name: Boston-Sahale Col
waypoints.note: Top of the glacier traverse beneath the Sharkfin face; gains the col between Sahale and Boston Peak before the final scramble.
waypoints.directions: Climb the upper glacier to a second crossing near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route late in the season. Later in summer the usual line goes right around the end of the bergschrund, then cuts back up and left to the Boston-Sahale col, the only low saddle at the top of the glacier.

waypoints.name: Sahale Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble up the summit block from the col; the true summit block has fixed anchors used by many parties to rappel back to the col.
waypoints.directions: From the col, traverse right (south) across a short but exposed snow slope with a rocky step, crampons and axe on and well back from any cornice, to the base of the summit block. Finish with about 60-70 ft of very exposed, loose Class 3 with 4th-class moves to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Boston Basin climbers' trailhead (Cascade River Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 22.5 miles to the small Boston Basin pullout, passing the Eldorado parking area at about mile 20. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is rough gravel.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
approach_variants.hours: 4-5 to camp, about 2 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing is the summit pyramid above the glacier, and the mistake to avoid is attacking it straight on.

From the top of the glacier you arrive under the southwest side of the summit block. Do not start up the steepest ground directly in front of you. Trend up and right to a flat ledge just below the top; the finish is a short chimney-like feature on the south side of the pyramid. You should find yourself on a system of solid but increasingly exposed class 3 ledges, not on a face.

The last confirmation is a short class 4 move — about twenty feet of it, one awkward crack or chimney-like exit that puts you through a notch in the summit rocks onto the top. There is a fixed rappel station at that spot, and finding a fixed anchor is the clearest proof from the ground that you are on the standard line and not a variation.

The trap is the dihedral. Left of the standard notch there is a steeper dihedral feature that reads as the obvious line; it goes at fourth to low fifth class on loose rock and wants gear. If you are looking at a clean-cut corner rather than a rubble ledge that leads around and right, you are on the harder variation.

In poor visibility: the block is small and unmistakable once you are at it, so the navigation problem is the glacier, not the rock. Late season the glacier surface is cut by meltwater runnels that look like crevasses and crevasses that look like runnels — parties report going up and climber's right, climbing diagonally across the gullies, because that side reads more reliably.

approach_variants.name: Car-to-car day push
approach_variants.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, long daylight
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When you could not get a permit for Sahale Glacier Camp, or want to skip the quota; a strong party can do it in one long day, carrying glacier gear the whole way.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical to the camp version — the pyramid above the top of the Sahale Glacier, gained by trending right to the ledge below the top and the short chimney-like exit on the south side at the fixed rappel station.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for roughly the first 10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel/dirt for the remaining ~13 miles to the trailhead; passable to standard cars in good conditions, high clearance helps in rough years

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to its end, about 22 to 23 miles from Marblemount, to the large parking lot at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at 3,600 feet. If you plan to stay overnight at Sahale Glacier Camp, note that the permit is quota-limited — get an early-access wilderness permit or a walk-up the day before at the Marblemount ranger station.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.directions: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the parking lot as it switchbacks steadily up through old-growth forest, roughly 1,800 ft in the first 2 miles, then eases across subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at about 3.7 miles.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.directions: At Cascade Pass take the left (north) fork signed for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, passing above Doubtful Lake. The final stretch above the Arm is loose scree and talus on cairns with real exposure, ending at the rock-walled tent pads of Sahale Glacier Camp.

waypoints.name: Sahale Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: From camp, rope up and climb the Sahale Glacier to the southwest base of the summit pyramid. A short, exposed stretch of steep snow and class 3-4 rock leads to a ledge just below the top, finished by an awkward chimney-like move onto the summit block.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass parking lot. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is gravel.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3 to camp, about 2.5 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
hazards: Wrong-gully error — the defining hazard of this approach, with a fatal precedent
Bergschrund or seracs barring the direct gully entry
Rockfall in the gully, natural and from parties above
Poor natural anchors — a boulder anchor failure caused the 2005 fatalities
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe traverse
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the most consequential base-finding problem on this list, and it has killed people.

The correct line: from a position on the glacier directly below the tower — not past it — a single gully breaks through the steep rock band. Follow it up to a snow patch or sloping terrace at the base of the tower. From that terrace, a short second gully leads to a notch, and the notch is the start of the Southeast Ridge. Some parties also describe a snow gully west of the tower that gives access to that same wide bench below the objective.

The test to apply before committing: does this gully put me on a terrace directly under the fin? If you are climbing a gully that trends away from being underneath the tower, you are in the wrong one. Being on rock is not evidence of being on route — there are similar-looking gullies here.

On 10 July 2005 a six-person party crossed the glacier, walked past the standard access gully and climbed a similar-looking gully further along. The traverse back toward the correct line put them under rockfall, which struck a climber; during the retreat rappel a natural boulder anchor failed. Three died and a fourth was seriously injured. Every subsequent description of this approach leads with the same instruction: identify the correct gully.

Carry a beta photo or a GPS track. In cloud, when you cannot see the fin above you, this approach should not be committed to on guesswork.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
hazards: Wrong-gully error, harder to rule out once the snow has gone
Loose scree and climber-triggered rockfall in the gully
Open moat at the glacier-rock junction
Rockfall from parties rappelling the descent line
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Late season, August to September, once the approach gully has melted out to loose scree; expect rockfall risk from parties above and a moat at the glacier edge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification rule does not change: the correct gully is the one directly beneath the tower that delivers you onto the sloping terrace at the fin's base, followed by a short gully to the notch that begins the Southeast Ridge.

Late season it is arguably harder to be sure, because the snow that made the gully obvious from a distance has gone and several dry rubble chutes look alike from the glacier. Rely on the view from lower down: the gully, terrace and notch are all visible from the approach trail and from camp, so fix the line in your head before you lose the perspective.

Descent parties commonly rappel part of the route and then off rock to the west of the approach gully, so a fixed station west of your gully is a supporting sign you are in the right corridor — but it is a weaker signal than the terrace itself.

road.name: Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15)
road.status: Winter closure: as of the park's Nov 9, 2026 update, cars stop at the gate at milepost 21; you may walk or ride a bike beyond it to the Boston Basin parking area at mile 22.5.

Expect pavement for roughly the first 10 miles and rough gravel after that. The park bars trailers past its boundary at mile 18 and any vehicle over 22 ft long or 8 ft wide, and advises against sedans and low-clearance cars.
road.seasonalGate: In a normal year the road is open through to the Cascade Pass trailhead by the end of June (early July after a big snow year or storm damage); outside that season the park may gate it at different points for winter, maintenance or emergencies.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the unsigned Boston Basin pullout, at roughly 3,200-3,400 feet. The upper road is prone to washouts, so check its status before you go. Park at the small, unsigned roadside pullout; there's no trailhead sign. Camping in Boston Basin requires an NPS wilderness permit, since it's a quota area, arranged through Marblemount.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin
waypoints.directions: From the pullout, walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then turn sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. It climbs through old growth across four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the low camps on the heather benches. A higher camp sits farther up on a meadow knoll around 6,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Base of southeast ridge
waypoints.directions: From camp, skirt the climber's-left side of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it high, then rope up and traverse east along the top of the glacier until you are directly beneath the tower. Climb the single gully that breaks the rock band there (snow early season, loose scree later) to a terrace at the tower's base, then a short second gully to the notch. If your gully does not lead onto a terrace directly under the fin, you are in the wrong one.

waypoints.name: Sharkfin Tower summit
waypoints.directions: From the notch, skirt the ridge on climber's right over large blocks and up a short dihedral to the crest, then follow the exposed crest and the upper blocks for about three pitches of low fifth class to the small summit.

approach_variants.name: Glacier flank traverse from the east ridge camp
approach_variants.notes: From the parking area on Cascade River Road, backtrack along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River, then take the steep unmaintained climbers' boot path up through old-growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine basin above. Camp on the rocks by the broad flat of the glacier — the standard camp for the ordinary east-ridge line — and traverse from there. Overnight stays need a free backcountry permit.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the glacier flank snow has consolidated but before the ground above the notch melts out to loose scree
hazards: The traverse to the base is steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier — crampons are mandatory
Ground above the ridge is broad and turns to loose scree when melted out
Glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear is required to reach camp at all
approach_variants.baseFinding: Seen from the glacier on the standard camp approach, this route is the left-hand skyline. The right-hand one is the ordinary way up — a broad snow crest leading to the summit arete — so the first check is simply which of the two skylines you are under. Pick the lowest point on the left skyline and traverse the flank of the glacier to it; that traverse is steep, exposed snow and crampons are not optional. The base is then proved by a single feature you can see from the snow before committing: an obvious crack running up the face directly above you to a U-shaped notch cut into the ridge crest. The crack and the U-notch are one thing and either alone is not enough. If there is no U-notch above the crack you have picked, you are too high or too far along the ridge, and the ground there rolls back into loose scree. If you are walking on broad snow with nothing but a snow crest above you, you are on the ordinary route and not on this climb at all.

road.name: Cascade River Road (from Marblemount) to Boston Basin/Eldorado trailhead area
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel with potholes and washboard; passenger cars can often reach mile ~18 (NP boundary) but a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for the final miles to the Eldorado TH/Boston Basin pulloff (~mile 20-21.7). Vulnerable to washouts/flooding closures, especially in spring and after heavy rain.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3-3.5 hours from Seattle to Marblemount, then 45 min-1+ hour further up Cascade River Road to the trailhead area.
road.seasonalGate: Only snow-cleared and opened each spring/early summer; check the NPS North Cascades road-conditions page before driving.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH
waypoints.directions: From Seattle, take I-5 north to WA-20 and follow the North Cascades Highway east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount. Turn south onto Cascade River Road and drive about 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20, at roughly 2,100 feet. The first 10 miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard. Any overnight stay needs a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, so either reserve one on Recreation.gov ahead of time or stop at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center on your way in for one of the limited walk-up spots.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek basin
waypoints.note: Upper basin, above the boulder fields. From here climb to the notch in the ridge between Eldorado Creek and Roush Creek, about 6,200 ft, and descend a short third-class gully into the Roush Creek basin at the foot of the Eldorado Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Walk back down the road a short way to cross the Cascade River, on a log or by fording; the crossing shifts from year to year. Follow the steep, unmaintained climbers' path up through old-growth forest east of Eldorado Creek to the boulder field near 4,000 ft, climb about 1,000 ft of boulders, and continue into the Eldorado Creek basin near 5,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Eldorado camp (Inspiration Glacier flat)
waypoints.note: Good camps on rocks near the broad flat of the Inspiration Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb to the notch in the ridge between Eldorado Creek and Roush Creek, about 6,200 ft, and descend a short third-class gully into the Roush Creek basin. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier to the broad flat where it meets the Inspiration Glacier, near 7,600 ft, and camp on the rocks at its edge.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak
waypoints.note: Broad, snow-covered ridge to the spectacular knife-edge summit; the standard/easiest route.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the glacier's flank (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline from camp, below an obvious crack leading to a U-shaped notch. Climb the crack to the notch, cross to the far side and climb cracks back to the knife-edge crest, follow the crest two pitches to a short downclimb, then scramble the broad upper ridge to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp
approach_variants.notes: From the small pullout on Cascade River Road, take the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the old mine roadbed, across several streams and out above treeline to the Boston Basin camps. The formation is visible and easily picked out from the basin, and the climb is a half-day outing on light packs from camp. Overnight parties need a wilderness permit for the basin.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, from an established camp in the basin
hazards: Route-finding here is markedly less obvious than on the other side of the formation — scout the line from the basin before committing
Exposed ridge with short fifth-class steps between fourth-class scrambling
Glacier and snow travel to reach the foot of the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: The formation is the cockscomb standing on the divide between the upper Forbidden basin and the Torment basin with its glacier — a small, sharply notched crest that reads as an M from below, which is where its name comes from, and it is unmistakable once you are up out of the basin. Two skylines run down off it and the whole question is which one you are under. The right-hand skyline is the other route on the formation; the left-hand one is this climb. The negative marker is exact and easy to check on the ground: the right-hand route is entered from a notch on the right of that skyline, and from that notch it gives three or four pitches of fourth class to the foot of a tower and then one short pitch to its top. If you are standing in a notch on the right-hand side of the formation looking at a tower, you are on the other route. This ridge is gained round the far end of the crest, is the longer and less obvious of the two, and parties consistently find the route-finding on it the harder part of the day.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road opposite Johannesburg Mountain.
waypoints.directions: From WA-20 in Marblemount, turn onto Cascade River Road and drive about 22 miles, paved at first and then gravel, to a small pullout on the left opposite Johannesburg Mountain at about 3,200 ft, shortly after milepost 22. If you reach the Cascade Pass road end you have gone too far. Overnight stays in Boston Basin need a North Cascades National Park wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Established camp area with a toilet; overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park wilderness permit.
waypoints.directions: Climb the steep, unmaintained climbers' path from the pullout along the old mine roadbed, across several streams and out above treeline to the Boston Basin high camp.

waypoints.name: Aiguille de l'M
waypoints.note: South Ridge (5.6) climbs the exposed skyline ridge visible from Boston Basin; classic half-day outing from high camp.
waypoints.directions: From camp, go up the snowfields to the foot of the formation's left-hand (south) skyline, leave the snow and climb about five pitches along the crest, passing a gendarme on its right side, to the summit.

approach_variants.name: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small unsigned Boston Basin pulloff near 3,200-3,300 ft. The old mining road runs about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, then an unmaintained but well-travelled boot path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams — top off bottles there — to treeline around 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on the knoll above the green meadows at 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully below the tower. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left give an alternate entry and rejoin the couloir about 100 ft up.

There is no separate approach to the Southeast Face. You reach it by climbing the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and rappelling.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, the same window as the Southeast Ridge; being steeper rock it sheds snow a little faster after an early-season storm
hazards: Getting into the wrong gully: on 10 July 2005 a six-person party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here, a climber was struck by rockfall during the roped traverse back toward the standard line, and minutes later a natural boulder anchor failed during the retreat rappel, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth
Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier
The two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains and no rap rings, and there is no anchor at all at the very base of pitch 1
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food canisters required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This face is not walked to. It is rappelled into — and that is the cleanest test on the whole tower. A party standing at its start has already climbed the first two pitches of the southeast ridge and made two rappels of about 75 ft each from the fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2. A party that walked to where it is standing is at the Southeast Ridge notch, one route to the side.

You can see the face from that notch, which is why the mix-up happens: the clean southeast face is visible from the base of the Southeast Ridge and looks approachable. It is not, from there.

Identify the ridge notch by its anchor, not by its shape: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 carries no chains and no rap rings. That absence is a positive identification, and it is also a planning fact — you will be leaving a biner, a ring or a short cord to get down.

Before any of that, get the approach gully right, because this is where people have died. Traverse east along the top of the Quien Sabe several hundred feet; the correct gully leads to a snow patch directly at the tower's base and then a short gully to the notch. A similar-looking gully nearby does not. If your gully does not deliver you to a snow patch at the foot of the tower, stop and re-check rather than continuing or traversing across — the 2005 accident happened during exactly that correction, not during the mistake.

Confirm on the first moves of the face itself: pitch 1 steps onto a detached block and then follows a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just left of the arete to a bolted anchor in a notch. If you are not standing on a detached block, you are not on this pitch.

road.name: Cascade River Road (from Marblemount), ~21.7 mi to the unsigned Boston Basin pulloff
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles, then gravel with potholes/washboard, narrow and steep near the end; high-clearance recommended for the final stretch to the ~3,200-3,300 ft pulloff. Vulnerable to washouts/flooding closures.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Turnout at old Diamond Mine Rd fork off Cascade River Rd; climbers trail to Boston Basin, Quien Sabe Glacier approach to Sharkfin Tower. Safety note: a 2005 accident occurred here from parties entering the wrong approach gully, resulting in fatalities.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small, unsigned Boston Basin pulloff at about 3,200-3,300 feet. It's a rough, sometimes rutted gravel road, so a bit of ground clearance helps. Park at the pulloff alongside the road. A Boston Basin wilderness permit is required for the trip.

waypoints.name: Sharkfin Tower Southeast Face
waypoints.directions: Hike to Boston Basin and on to high camp, then contour up talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier, rope up and traverse east several hundred feet to the correct gully below the tower. Climb the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge, then make two rappels of about 75 ft from the anchor at the top of pitch 2 to reach the foot of the face's crack pitch.

waypoints.name: Sharkfin Tower summit
waypoints.note: This is Sharkfin Tower's summit, not Mount Torment's — a different, neighboring Boston Basin peak. The coordinate matches the summit waypoint already on this peak's sibling Southeast Ridge route.
waypoints.directions: Climb the face's two pitches (5.10- then 5.9) to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Boston Basin climbers' trailhead (Cascade River Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 22.5 miles to the small Boston Basin pullout, passing the Eldorado parking area at about mile 20. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is rough gravel.

approach_variants.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
approach_variants.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the toe of the buttress at the foot of a prominent, often year-round snow gully, and the gully is located by descending — it starts about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

At the top of that gully there is a fork, and it is the one thing on this peak most worth getting right. This route goes around to the right. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes straight up from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

The strongest negative test is published as a warning and it is worth carrying verbatim: do not climb directly below the ridge crest at the start. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 overhanging terrain on loose rock. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

Confirm on pitch one: it is a full rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly right, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

And confirm by which col you crossed: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel the rest of the way; the Eldorado Creek trailhead is at about mile 20 and the road continues to the Cascade Pass trailhead. NPS listed the road as open on its road-conditions page as of 3 July 2026 and no longer lists the June 2026 vehicle closure at Eldorado Creek. Washouts and landslides have closed this road at Eldorado Creek repeatedly over the years, so check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
road.driveNote: Not suitable for low-clearance vehicles beyond the pavement; vehicles/trailers over 22 ft or 8 ft wide prohibited beyond mile 18.
road.seasonalGate: Typically snow-gated in winter/spring; usually opens to Cascade Pass trailhead by late June in a normal year.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the East Ridge; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at about road mile 20, elevation roughly 2,100 ft, and park in the trailhead lot. The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp option after the first two talus fields and a waterfall crossing.
waypoints.directions: Follow the climbers' path up the west side of Eldorado Creek, climbing steeply through old-growth forest with no water to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Continue up the talus, re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, and carry on up to the open basin.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the flat glacier shelf used to stage the Inspiration/McAllister glacier traverse.
waypoints.directions: Switchback up past 6,000 ft and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water). From the basin climb 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft, rope up, and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north across Inspiration Glacier to this col, then drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From high camp, rope up and cross north over the Inspiration Glacier to the col at about 8,000 ft where it meets the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Descend the McAllister Glacier toward its southwest gap; navigate visible crevasses, especially late-season.
waypoints.directions: From the col, drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier and descend toward its southwest gap, threading the visible crevasses, which open up late in the season.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Lowest gap on the SW side of the glacier; cross to the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.
waypoints.directions: Continue across the McAllister to the Marble Creek-McAllister pass, the lowest gap on the southwest side of the glacier, and cross onto the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.

waypoints.name: Base of Southwest Buttress gully
waypoints.note: A snow-filled gully roughly 700 vertical feet below the pass leads to the start of the buttress climbing.
waypoints.directions: From the pass, descend about 700 ft on the Marble Creek side to the foot of the prominent gully, which often holds snow all year.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: 9-pitch, Grade III, 5.7-5.8 buttress tops out on the true summit after a left-leaning corner on the upper ridge.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully to the toe of the buttress, minding the moat at the base of the rock, then follow about nine pitches of 5.7-5.8 cracks, slabs and gendarme traverses to the knife-edge summit ridge.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.

access.fees: Backcountry camping fee is $10/person plus a one-time $6 non-refundable reservation fee, charged mid-May through early October; no charge outside that window and none for youth 15 and under. There is no park entrance fee for North Cascades NP.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay in the park; get it at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount ((360) 854-7245) or the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin. About 60% of sites are reservable in advance on Recreation.gov; the remaining ~40% are walk-up only, issued in person up to 24 hours ahead.
access.closures: Camping is prohibited at Park Creek Pass itself to protect fragile alpine turf — plan to camp at Thunder Basin, Park Creek, or the high basin instead. Trail washouts have periodically hit the Bridge Creek/North Fork corridor near Stehekin, sometimes requiring a bike-and-hike detour around damaged sections — check current NPS trail conditions before relying on that approach. A major December 2025 atmospheric-river flood also severely damaged Stehekin's Company Creek Road, power, and wastewater infrastructure, disrupting North Cascades Lodge services and the Stehekin shuttle/ferry into the 2026 season; an interim road repair was completed in June 2026 but services remain limited — check the NPS Stehekin Flood Response Update page before planning the Stehekin/Park Creek approach. Thunder Creek Fire: North Cascades National Park's fire-closure list (updated September 14, 2026; no end date given) closes the Thunder Creek Trail from the Fisher Creek Trail junction to Park Creek Pass for the Thunder Creek Fire, along with Junction Camp, Skagit Queen Camp and Thunder Basin Camp (hiker and stock sites), and prohibits cross-country travel from the closed trail. The Thunder Creek approach cannot be used past the Fisher Creek junction while this stands. The same list also closes the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge, the High Bridge area, and the Pacific Crest Trail from the park boundary to Bridge Creek Camp for the Sisi Fire, so the Stehekin/High Bridge approach is closed as well. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

overnight_permit.where: Reserve a night-by-night itinerary online via Recreation.gov during the early-access lottery, or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites) at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount up to 24 hours ahead.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
camps: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and hard patches on the basin traverse into early August
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit with real fall consequences
Aging in-situ slings at the crux that need backing up before use
Easy to drift off-line in poor visibility; the route is indistinguishable from the neighbouring peak's below 7,400 ft
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation for a serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The most important thing to know about this approach is that below 7,400 ft it is indistinguishable from Goode Mountain's. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

The counting test is the notch, and the word is right-most. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the right-most one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

Cross to the north side of that notch and the ground changes character completely: a fun ledge traverse on the backside of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. If you have not crossed to the north side, you have not found the ledge traverse, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

Confirm on the ledge: it includes a squeeze under a slight overhang, and there are in-situ slings at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

The last move is a choice, not a crux: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its left side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

And know which top you want: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the easternmost is the true high point.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.
hazards: Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail approach
Lake crossing and shuttle schedule: a missed connection puts you a day behind
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn
Lingering snow on the basin traverse into early August
Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, rockfall onto parties below
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When the lake boat and High Bridge shuttle schedule fits, this skips the long Thunder Creek walk and reaches the Park Creek trail with the least distance on foot.

approach_variants.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.

Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Colonial Creek CG, or Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass Trailhead, or the Lake Chelan ferry/floatplane to Stehekin, depending on approach chosen.
road.status: SR-20 is paved; Cascade River Road is gravel beyond the pavement's end and has had early-season washout closures in some years; Stehekin has no outside road access at all — it's reached only by the Lake Chelan passenger ferry, floatplane, or a very long trail.
road.driveNote: For the Thunder Creek approach, the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead is on SR-20 about 24 miles east of Marblemount, just past milepost 130.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 over Washington/Rainy Pass typically closes for winter (roughly mid-November through April, weather dependent); Cascade River Road usually opens later in spring than the highway.

waypoints.name: Colonial Creek Campground Trailhead
waypoints.note: Drive-to trailhead in Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130; the Thunder Creek Trail leaves from the south end of the campground near the amphitheater. The alternative southern start is by boat to Stehekin and shuttle to High Bridge, then up the Park Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead, the start of the most commonly used approach into this basin. From there the Thunder Creek Trail — an easy, mostly forested stock and hiker trail — climbs only about 600 feet over its first 13 miles up-valley. Two alternate approaches reach the same high basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek, also starting from SR-20, or a southern approach by boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required, and if you're using the Stehekin ferry or shuttle, both run on a limited schedule — typically mid-June through September — so check timetables and reserve the permit before planning dates.

waypoints.name: Skagit Queen Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp near old Skagit Queen mine workings where the trail steepens into switchbacks; reliable creek water, common first- or second-night stop.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 — an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail with only about 600 ft of gain — roughly 13 miles up-valley, passing McAllister Camp near mile 6 and Junction Camp near mile 9.5.

waypoints.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
Park Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Trail high point in the notch between Mt. Logan and Mt. Buckner; camping is prohibited at the pass itself to protect fragile meadows, so continue on or camp just below it.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley past Thunder Basin Camp around mile 16.5, then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple of miles beyond; it switchbacks up through meadows to the pass.

waypoints.name: North-side exposed ledge traverse
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledge system traversing the backside of the summit towers, including a slight overhang requiring a squeeze-under move; most parties fix a line here.
waypoints.directions: From the cirque, ascend the long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks, staying right of the horn-shaped rock gully at about 8,000 ft to be in the correct gully. This slope is the approach's main hazard — helmets on and space the party out for rockfall and unstable footing. Around 70 ft of Class 3 scrambling reaches the notch, and it is the right-most of the notches in the summit rocks; cross to the north side of it to gain the ledge.

waypoints.name: Summit crux crack
waypoints.note: 15-foot crack (Class 4 to low 5th) leads to the fixed rappel anchor used for the descent; rope up or belay through this section.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ledge roughly 70 ft across the backside of the tower — two or three Class 4 moves, full exposure, and a squeeze under a slight overhang; many parties fix a line. The ledge widens and holds loose rock, so move carefully, then continue across the summit tower's backside to the small spur at the foot of the crack.

waypoints.name: Storm King summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the 15-ft solid Class 4 face crack, or wrap around its left side on easier Class 3 blocks; both reach the register and the fixed rappel slings. A final short Class 3 pitch tops out. Two points above 8,520 ft sit east of the triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit — the easternmost is the true high point.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee, summer season (mid-May-early October); free the rest of the year.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Same NPS backcountry permit system as the rest of Southeast Mox Peak — required for any overnight; reserve via Recreation.gov or obtain in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
access.closures: Fire-related area closures have affected Ross Lake/Perry Creek access in some (unrelated, later) seasons — check current North Cascades NP conditions before a trip
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex / Ross Lake National Recreation Area (NPS)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota, paid reservation
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov (early-access lottery in March, then general on-sale at least 2 days ahead); about 40% of sites are held for walk-up permits issued in person up to 24 hours before the trip at a Wilderness Information Center.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to the Little Beaver landing, then the Perry Creek drainage
approach_variants.notes:
Access starts on the water. From the trailhead near milepost 134 walk down to the resort and take its water taxi, or paddle, a long way up the lake to the dock at its northern end. From the dock follow the maintained but lightly travelled valley trail west, through cedar and fir with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, to a camp with a three-sided log shelter - the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward this massif.

Beyond the shelter there is no trail. This is a genuinely serious approach and not a formality: the first ascent party needed two full days in the rain from the lake to the base - four and a half miles of trail, then roughly fourteen hours of brush and creek travel - and described it as one of the worst approaches in the range. Expect cold fords, soaked gear, and skin torn by devil's club and slide alder - the plant the route is named for. Water is everywhere and should be treated.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn; the creek travel is the governing factor rather than the climbing
hazards: a water taxi or a paddle up a long lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
cold creek fords and continuously wet travel
devil's club and slide alder dense enough to stop progress on the wrong bank
avalanche paths on the north side of the drainage
moats between snowfield and rock at the toe of the face
a base days from any road with a very long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The shelter is the last fixed object you will see - a three-sided log structure at the camp. Everything after it is read off the creek.

Stay in or beside the creekbed itself as long as it lets you. Rock-hopping and easy scrambling in the bed is the fastest travel available and it holds to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the channel and forces you up a bank.

The one decision of the approach is which bank, and it has a right answer: take the south, true-left side. It holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths. The north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket - so if you are swimming through continuous alder with no let-up and no open timber, you are on the wrong bank and the fix is to cross rather than to keep pushing.

The confirmation that you chose right comes as a change of vegetation: above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber, and travel speed roughly triples. If your speed has not changed, you have not cleared the band.

The base is the cirque at the head of the drainage, beneath the connecting ridge that runs to the summit, with talus and season-dependent snowfields and moats guarding the toe of the face. The face itself is the feature - a continuous wall of well over two thousand feet rising straight out of the cirque. If the ground above you is broken into ledges and gullies rather than a single sustained face, you are under the flanking ground and not under the route.

Watch the moat where snow meets rock at the toe; how bad it is depends entirely on the season and it decides where the first pitch can start.

road.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (off SR-20 near milepost 134), then Ross Lake Resort water taxi
road.status: SR-20 to Ross Dam Trailhead is paved; hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the water taxi across the reservoir before a long multi-day cross-country approach.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to Ross Dam, plus the water taxi crossing and a multi-day wilderness approach.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: US-side approach, opposite the Depot Creek approach used for the West Ridge/Beckey route. Climbers take a water taxi (or boat, portaging Diablo Lake to Ross Lake) up Ross Lake ~15 miles to the Little Beaver landing/dock, then hike/bushwhack up the Perry Creek drainage to reach the base of Southeast Mox Peak's East Face.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead near milepost 134, about 14 miles past Newhalem, and park in the small lot. From here a trail drops about 1 mile through forest toward Ross Dam; at the bottom, turn right on the gravel road to the lakeshore, where a phone on the last power pole calls Ross Lake Resort for the water taxi, which must be reserved in advance.

waypoints.name: Southeast Mox Peak (Hard Mox) summit / East Face high point
waypoints.directions: Take the water taxi about 15 miles up Ross Lake to the Little Beaver dock and follow the Little Beaver Trail west about 5 miles to Perry Creek Camp. Then go trailless south up the Perry Creek drainage, in the creekbed to about 3,600 ft and on the south (true left) bank above it, to the cirque at the toe of the East Face; plan on two days to the base. Climb the face to the summit.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Newhalem, drive SR-20 east about 14 miles; the trailhead parking is on the right between mileposts 134 and 135.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee for advance permits (youth 15 and under free); no park entrance fee at North Cascades NP.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.

access.permit: Overnight backcountry/wilderness permit required year-round for any camping on this route. About 60% of designated camps/zones are reservable in advance on Recreation.gov (requires watching a safety video and emailing the WIC within 3 days of your trip to confirm); the park holds roughly 40% of sites for walk-up permits issued in person at the WIC (Marblemount) or Glacier Public Service Center, day-of or day-before only.
access.closures: Colonial Creek Campground and the Thunder Creek Trailhead are reached via SR-20, which stays open essentially year-round this far west (well before the highway's seasonal closure gate near Ross Dam, MP 134); Cascade River Road to Eldorado Creek is not needed for this route unless linking into the Inspiration Traverse. The original Thunder Creek Trail bridge near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017 and has not been replaced — parties cross on logs a short way upstream of the old bridge site.
access.seasonal: SR-20 stays open to Colonial Creek Campground year-round; the highway's winter closure is further east near Ross Dam.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit — limited, with a fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center up to a day ahead. Camps above Thunder Creek fall in cross-country zones.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek, Borealis Lake and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the large lot above the boat ramp at Colonial Creek, follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south to McAllister Camp; the old bridge near mile 6.6 is gone and the crossing is now on logs a short way upstream of the old site. Across the creek pick up the unmaintained boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and blowdown up the north ridge past a viewpoint that gives the first look at the peaks. Continue through forest and heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the base camp. From camp rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle; it has retreated into an upper and a lower tier separated by slabs and cliffs, to the col.
approach_variants.season: July and August are best; earlier ascents need ice technique, and the south-facing snow above the col softens dangerously through the day
hazards: Crevasses on the Borealis Glacier, worse late in the season
Brushy, poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp
Afternoon softening of the south-facing snow finger — start early
Class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges above the snow
approach_variants.baseFinding: Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and this peak, is the base, and which way you turn on it is the whole test. Standing on the col, Primus is the peak to the west and this one is to the east; the route turns east. Above the pass on that side a single steep snow finger runs up roughly 200 ft. It is unmistakable from the col and there is no second candidate, and it is the entry to the climb. Above the snow the ground becomes rock ramps and ledges, class 3 to 4, following the west ridge to a bouldery summit. If you have left the col heading west onto a broad class 2-3 ridge, you are climbing Primus instead. If you are still threading crevasses on slabby, tiered ice below the col, you have not reached the pass at all — the glacier here is split into two tiers by slabs and cliffs and it is the upper tier that runs to the col.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to Colonial Creek Campground (Thunder Creek Trailhead) — the standard approach for this route. Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek Trailhead is only relevant if linking this peak into the longer Inspiration Traverse.
road.status: SR-20 is paved all the way to Colonial Creek Campground and open essentially year-round, since the campground sits well west of the highway's seasonal closure gate near Ross Dam (MP 134). Cascade River Road to Eldorado Creek (used only for the Inspiration Traverse) is paved partway then gravel and has a history of storm-driven washouts.
road.driveNote: Trailhead parking is at Colonial Creek Campground directly off SR-20; a valid park pass/fee is required and rangers record license plates.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 closes east of Ross Dam (MP 134) in winter, well beyond Colonial Creek Campground/Thunder Creek Trailhead (MP 130), which stays accessible essentially year-round; snow at higher elevations still restricts the climbing route itself to summer/early fall.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead (Colonial Creek Campground, South Loop)
waypoints.note: This is a legitimately long/remote approach (24-mile round trip: Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister camp, off-trail to Borealis Lake, across Borealis Glacier to Lucky Pass)
waypoints.directions: Colonial Creek Campground sits on SR-20 at Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount. Turn in on the campground's south side and park in the large lot above the boat ramp, around 1,240 ft. That lot is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead, and the maintained Thunder Creek Trail runs south from it.

waypoints.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
McAllister Camp
waypoints.note: Backcountry stock camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek; the climbers' boot path up the north ridge starts on the far side of Thunder Creek. Coordinates approximate.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south about 6.5 miles to McAllister Camp.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek log crossing
waypoints.note: The original footbridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties cross on logs about a quarter mile upstream of the old bridge site, then follow the far bank back downstream to the start of the climbers' path. The logs shift from year to year. Coordinates approximate.
waypoints.directions: Continue south on the Thunder Creek Trail past McAllister Camp and the old washed-out bridge site, about a quarter mile, to the log jam, and cross Thunder Creek.

waypoints.name: Ridge viewpoint
waypoints.note: Boot path up the north ridge passes a viewpoint here with the first views of Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Coordinates approximate.
waypoints.directions: On the far bank pick up the unmaintained boot path at the first fork and climb steeply up the north ridge through brush and blowdown to a viewpoint near 4,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Borealis Lake camp
waypoints.note: Standard base camp on a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. Elevation and coordinates are approximate — not precisely surveyed.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the boot path through forest and then heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the standard base camp below the Borealis Glacier.

waypoints.name: Lucky Pass (Primus-Tricouni col)
waypoints.note: Reached via roped travel up the Borealis Glacier, which has retreated and split into upper/lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs. Elevation and coordinates are approximate.
waypoints.directions: Rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle. The glacier is split into a lower and an upper tier by slabs and cliffs; the upper tier leads to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni.

waypoints.name: Tricouni Peak
waypoints.directions: From the col turn east, away from Primus, and climb the single steep snow finger about 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then scramble class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges up the west ridge to the bouldery summit.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Start at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount) and park in the large lot above the boat ramp on the campground's south side — this is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead.

access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: No permit needed for day climbing; a backcountry permit from the Glacier Public Service Center is required only for overnight stays within North Cascades National Park
access.closures: FR-32 has periodically had flood/storm damage limiting access for larger vehicles beyond ~mile 5.2 — check Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving; stock animals restricted to Aug 1–Oct 31 on the trail.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Ranger District / Glacier Public Service Center)
access.land_manager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Ranger District / Glacier Public Service Center)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency Pass (Washington State Discover Pass is NOT valid)

road.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FS-32), off Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542)
road.status: FS-32 is a maintained forest road running 4 miles from SR-542 to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at road's end; generally passable to standard cars in season.
road.driveNote: Roughly 2-2.5 hours from Seattle/Bellingham via SR-542 and FS-32 to the trailhead; the peak itself is only a few minutes' walk up-trail from the parking area.

waypoints.name: Mamie Peak crag (near base of Ellation)

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From SR-542 12.5 miles east of Glacier, up Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32) 5.3 miles to the road-end trailhead (~3,120 ft), via the Ruth Creek valley
